entry.title: SAP‑RPT‑TS: SAP's new Time Series Foundation Model
entry.content:
1. Introduction

SAP has released a new Time Series Foundation Model, SAP‑RPT‑TS. Its key features are:

  • Zero‑shot forecasting: pre‑trained and ready to use, no algorithm selection, no parameter tuning, no series analysis, just forecast.
  • Small, fast, and accurate: ~28M parameters, lightweight and CPU‑friendly, with strong benchmark results.
  • Relational data + covariates: supports multiple targets and past and future covariates of different data types, and provides point forecasts, quantiles, and prediction intervals.
  • Unique capabilities: multi‑target cross‑learning, horizons of up to 1024 steps, and massive multi‑series forecasting (tens of thousands of series, e.g. product × store).
  • Two ways to run: on SAP AI Core or in the SAP HANA Cloud database.

Why we built it. Time‑series forecasting is a constant need across SAP applications: demand planning, inventory optimization, financial and operational planning, and more. Traditionally, each of these use cases needs its own model, trained and maintained separately. SAP‑RPT‑TS removes that overhead: as a foundation model it forecasts zero‑shot, so a new series can be predicted without any training. It is deliberately designed for CPU execution (cost‑effective, no GPU required) and runs both inside SAP HANA Cloud and on SAP AI Core, keeping data within your boundary.

How it works. SAP‑RPT‑TS is pre‑trained on tens of terabytes of time‑series data that mirror the patterns typical of SAP business scenarios. Given historical observations and optional covariates, it returns point forecasts and prediction intervals for each forecast step. 

This blog post focuses on getting you started quickly: Section 2 presents benchmark results; Section 3 shows how to use each deployment option.

 

2. Evaluation and benchmarks

These results come from SAP’s internal evaluations on FEV-Bench and GIFT-Eval using each suite’s tasks and metrics. They have not been submitted to the official leaderboards. The notebook runs the SAP‑RPT‑TS evaluations through the SAP AI Core REST API.

Leading accuracy on FEV‑Bench. FEV‑Bench is a realistic time‑series forecasting benchmark of 100 tasks across 7 real‑world domains, with a deliberate emphasis on exogenous covariates (static, known‑dynamic, and historical‑dynamic). SAP-RPT-TS achieves the lowest mean absolute scaled error (MASE), about 1.41, and the lowest scaled quantile loss (SQL) among the models shown in Fig. 1.

Fig.1. Fev‑Bench: MASE (left) and SQL (right); lower is better

First‑tier on GIFT‑Eval. GIFT‑Eval is a general evaluation suite for zero‑shot forecasting with time‑series foundation models, spanning 23 datasets, 7 domains, and 10 sampling frequencies, and assessing univariate and multivariate forecasting across short/medium/long horizons. In Fig. 2, SAP-RPT-TS ranks near the top on MASE and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), with a substantially smaller model than the leader.

Fig.2. GIFT‑Eval: MASE (left) and CRPS (right); lower is better

Small model, low inference latency. In this comparison, SAP-RPT-TS has the fewest parameters, about 28 million, and one of the lowest inference latencies (Figs. 3 and 4). Compared with models that run from hundreds of millions to billions of parameters and are several times slower, it reaches comparable accuracy at significantly lower cost. For enterprise forecasting over thousands of series that must be recomputed frequently, this combination of "small size + low latency + high accuracy" translates into a significant total‑cost‑of‑ownership (TCO) advantage.

Fig.3. Inference latency in seconds.

 

Fig.4. Model size, measured by parameter count

 

 

3. Getting started

The examples use a synthetic dataset with 365 daily observations for one building. The target is energy_consumption_kwh, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). The covariates are:

  • Future covariates: temperature_c, humidity_pct, solar_irradiance_kwh_m2, wind_speed_ms, is_weekend, and is_holiday. Their values are supplied for the forecast horizon. Calendar values are known in advance; the example assumes weather values are also available. For production forecasts, supply weather forecasts available at prediction time.
  • Past covariate: occupancy_rate, supplied only for the historical period and set to NULL for the forecast horizon in the PAL input table.

We hold out the final 14 days for forecasting. In the PAL input table, their target values are set to NULL, while future covariates remain populated. Both deployment options use the same dataset; the REST request separates historical observations from future covariates. Fig. 5 shows the first three rows of the input table.

Fig.5. The first three rows of the input table

 

 

Path one: SAP HANA Cloud PAL (in‑database)

If your data is in SAP HANA Cloud, HANA Predictive Analysis Library (PAL) lets you run forecasts directly in the database.

Prerequisites: access to SAP HANA Cloud with PAL enabled. The snippets below come from the linked sample notebook. 

The model supports multiple targets, but the QRC 3/2026 PAL TSFM operator accepts one target column per call, with optional covariates. For joint forecasting of multiple targets, use the SAP AI Core REST API. PAL support is planned for QRC 4/2026.

Prepare a table with an ordering column (ID or timestamp), one target column, and optional covariate columns. Sort the observations by the ordering column, then append one row per forecast step with the target set to NULL. Each series can contain up to 8,192 historical observations, with a forecast horizon of up to 1,024 steps.

SQL example, with history and future rows supplied in one call:

-- TSFM_ENERGY_TBL: target ENERGY_CONSUMPTION_KWH is NULL for the final 14 rows.
-- Future covariates have values for all 14 forecast steps.
-- Past covariate is NULL over horizon.

DO BEGIN
  DECLARE emptyModel TABLE (id INTEGER, value NVARCHAR(5000));

  DECLARE params TABLE (
    PARAM_NAME   NVARCHAR(256),
    INT_VALUE    INTEGER,
    DOUBLE_VALUE DOUBLE,
    STRING_VALUE NVARCHAR(5000)
  );

  params = SELECT 'OUTPUT_PREDICTION_INTERVAL' AS PARAM_NAME, 1 AS INT_VALUE, NULL AS DOUBLE_VALUE, NULL AS STRING_VALUE
  FROM DUMMY
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'CONFIDENCE_LEVEL', NULL, 0.9, NULL
  FROM DUMMY
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'PIPELINE', NULL, NULL, '{"TSFM": {"args": {}, "inputs": {"data": "ROWDATA"}}}'
  FROM DUMMY;

  data = SELECT "ID", "energy_consumption_kwh", "temperature_c", "humidity_pct",
                "solar_irradiance_kwh_m2", "wind_speed_ms",
                "is_weekend", "is_holiday", "occupancy_rate"
         FROM TSFM_ENERGY_TBL
         ORDER BY "ID";

  CALL _SYS_AFL.PAL_PIPELINE_PREDICT(:data, :emptyModel, :params, result, stat);

  SELECT * FROM :result;
END;

With the Python Machine Learning Client for SAP HANA (hana-ml), run the same forecast with Pipeline.predict:

from hana_ml.algorithms.pal.pipeline import Pipeline
# SAP-RPT-TS is exposed as the TSFM pipeline operator. 
# skip_fit=True uses the pretrained model without fitting it to this dataset.
# hdf: the input table containing history and future rows with NULL targets.
# COVARIATES: all covariate columns; only future covariates have horizon values.
pipe = Pipeline(pipeline={'TSFM': {'args': {}, 'inputs': {'data': 'ROWDATA'}}})
result = pipe.predict(data=hdf, key='ID', exog=COVARIATES, skip_fit=True, output_prediction_interval=1, confidence_level=0.9)
forecast = result.collect()

Reading the result: the output table gives, for each future time point, the point forecast (forecast column), the lower/upper confidence bounds (lower/upper columns). To forecast thousands of series in one go, switch to the Massive variant (MassivePipeline / PAL_MASSIVE_PIPELINE_PREDICT), which processes them in parallel by group key.

Fig. 6 shows the 14-day forecast for IDs 352 through 365. Fig. 7 compares it with recent history and held-out actual values.

Fig.6. Result table.

 

Fig.7. Forecast plot

 

 

Path two: SAP AI Core (REST interface, as a service)

SAP‑RPT‑TS is also available through generative AI Hub in SAP AI Core under the model name sap‑rpt‑ts. Use this path when you call from an application or service, or when your data is outside SAP HANA Cloud. Send a POST request to $DEPLOYMENT_URL/predict to generate probabilistic forecasts for one or more series.

Prerequisites: in AI Core, create a deployment configuration with executableId aicore-sap and model name sap‑rpt‑ts, start the deployment, and retrieve the deployment URL. Include both an Authorization: Bearer $AUTH_TOKEN header and an AI-Resource-Group header in every request. See the SAP-RPT-TS documentation for setup instructions and the sample notebook for the complete example. 

The following is the request payload for the energy consumption example:

payload = {
    "horizon": 14,
    "data": [{
        "timestamp": hist["date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist(),
        "target":    [hist["energy_consumption_kwh"].tolist()],
        "past_covariates":   {c: hist[c].tolist() for c in COVARIATES},
        "future_covariates": {c: fut[c].tolist()  for c in FUTURE_COVARIATES},
    }],
    "options": {"confidence_interval": 0.9},
}
out = client.rest_client.post(
    path=_predict_path, body=payload, convert_body_to_camel_case=False
)

The request requires horizon and data; each item in data must include historical target values in target. The timestamp field is optional but recommended. Supply historical covariate values in past_covariates and values available over the forecast horizon in future_covariates. Set options.confidence_interval to request a prediction interval; 0.9 specifies a 90% interval.

Response (excerpt):

{
  "result": [[[528.6, 548.9, 535.9, ...]]], // [n_series][n_variates][horizon]
  "confidence_interval_output": [[[[496.98, 513.8, 503.0, ...],// [n_series][n_variates][2][horizon]
                                    [561.05, 579.4, 564.6, ...]]]],  //   index 0 = lower, 1 = upper
  "result_timestamp": [["2023-12-18", "2023-12-19", "2023-12-20", ...]],
  "detected_interval":         [{"unit": "day", "value": 1}],
  ......  
}

The response contains the following fields. The result[series][variate][step] is the point forecast; confidence_interval_output[series][variate][0 or 1][step] gives lower/upper bounds; result_timestamp holds the forecast timestamp; detected_interval is the automatically detected sampling period. 

 

4. Summary

SAP-RPT-TS delivers accurate, probabilistic forecasts out of the box, with no per-use-case training and a small, CPU‑friendly footprint. Use PAL to forecast directly in SAP HANA Cloud, or the SAP AI Core REST API to integrate forecasting into applications and services. Start with the sample notebooks, then explore covariates and forecasting across multiple series.

 

References

  1. HANA Cloud  PAL : TSFM
  2. Python Machine Learning Client for SAP HANA : TSFM Pipeline Operator
  3. SAP AI Core : SAP‑RPT‑TS
  4. Sample notebooks
  5. FEV-Bench paper 
  6. GIFT-Eval paper

entry.title: Zero-shot time series forecasting with SAP-RPT-TS in SAP HANA Cloud and SAP AI Core
entry.content:
SAP is expanding its tabular AI capabilities with updates to the SAP-RPT AI model family, which will help companies harness structured data for faster, more accurate predictions. As part of the SAP Business AI Platform, these innovations provide additional context that supports the ability of AI to reason and take appropriate action.

While large language models (LLMs) are powerful tools for handling unstructured data, they often struggle with the structured data that is critical to everyday business processes and decisions. Tabular AI is designed to handle this kind of data — it enables AI to process, understand, and make predictions using structured data found in business applications, databases, and other sources.

SAP was an early mover in tabular AI with its 2025 launch of the SAP-RPT-1 AI model and continues to bring new models and capabilities to market for AI developers, data teams, and business users.

 

Introducing SAP-RPT-TS: time series forecasting joins the SAP-RPT AI model family

Time series forecasting is now unlocked with the new SAP-RPT-TS tabular foundation model, the latest and key expansion of the SAP-RPT AI model family. Here is what makes it distinct:

  • Pretrained foundation model. SAP-RPT-TS is a Relational Pre-trained Transformer (RPT) model. This removes the need to collect training datasets, manage compute infrastructure, or endure cycles of model experimentation, tuning, monitoring, and retraining.
  • Zero-shot business forecasting. SAP-RPT-TS provides a true zero-shot forecasting experience with no model training or tuning involved. By supplying a snapshot of historical data using in-context learning, the forecast is generated on-the-fly at predict time, enabling predictions across key enterprise indicators such as demand, sales, and operational metrics. It can help answer questions like: How does demand move next month? Where is inventory projected to run short? How does revenue develop across regions going forward?
  • Probabilistic predictions. The model produces forecasts grounded in the provided context data, returning calibrated prediction intervals that quantify uncertainty out-of-the-box, not just point estimates. This reduces the risk of costly over- or under-prediction decisions.
  • Flexible and resilient data handling. SAP-RPT-TS handles a wide range of forecast scenarios: univariate and multivariate series, both past and known-future covariates, and multiple targets with and without cross-learning. It automatically manages gaps and missing values in the series, and detects seasonality, trends, and the influence of covariates to improve accuracy. Support for intermittent time series is already on the roadmap for the next model update.
  • High quality, fast and lightweight. On enterprise data, SAP-RPT-TS yields predictions that are mostly superior to state-of-the-art narrow AI forecast models built specifically for such tasks. It delivers low-latency instant forecasts from within SAP HANA Cloud or SAP AI Core, served from a cost-effective CPU environment, with no expensive GPU hardware required.

 

Consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP HANA Cloud

Developers and business users can immediately access the model through SAP HANA Cloud or SAP AI Core.  To use SAP-RPT-TS directly from the database, first ensure that NLP services are enabled within your HANA Cloud instance configuration, and that the instance is version 2026.28 (Q3 2026) or newer.

In the current release, SAP-RPT-TS is accessible through the TSFM operator for PAL AutoML / Pipeline models (TSFM in hana_ml 2.30). There are two ways to use it. 

  • Use the PIPELINE PREDICT function with the TSFM operator: in skip-fit mode for instant zero-shot time series forecasts:
  • Use the AutoML FIT function with the TSFM operator: which simply allows to use it alongside classic time series operators (ARIMA, BSTS, AMTSA, HGBT-TS, MLR-TS, and others) within the AutoML Time Series scenario, where it is evaluated as a candidate model and selected only when it delivers the best forecast.

 

The screenshot above captures this in practice: a PAL pipeline configured for skip-fit mode, and the resulting output showing calibrated prediction intervals returned alongside the historical series, with no training step required. What stands out is how little code is involved. A handful of lines using hana_ml is all it takes to generate a production-quality time series forecast directly from SAP HANA Cloud.

More details on consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP HANA Cloud can be found in the companion blog post by xinchen   SAP‑RPT‑TS SAP's new Time Series Foundation Model, incl. a sample notebook.

 

Consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP AI Core 

SAP-RPT-TS is also available directly through SAP AI Core via the foundation-models scenario. Getting started requires creating a configuration and then a deployment using executableId: aicore-sap and modelName: sap-rpt-ts-1.0, or latest to always reference the newest model version. From there, the model is consumed through standard REST API calls, with no infrastructure to provision and no training jobs to manage. Examples covering a range of forecasting scenarios and input structures are provided in the example payloads documentation 

.

SAP-RPT-TS in SAP Integrated Business Planning for Demand

The first SAP application to integrate SAP-RPT-TS is SAP Integrated Business Planning for Demand (or IBP, generally available in Q1 2027 release update). Planners can use SAP-RPT-TS alongside any other algorithm in statistical forecasting, running it exactly as they do today with any other algorithm and reviewing the results directly in their planning views. No new tool, no exports, no coding.

The demo above shows this experience end-to-end: a planner running SAP-RPT-TS as one of the active forecast methods in IBP, selecting it, running it, and comparing its output against other models within the same familiar interface. The integration is seamless precisely because SAP-RPT-TS fits into existing workflows rather than replacing them.

 

Try SAP-RPT-TS free

Beyond the API and SAP AI Core, SAP-RPT-TS can be explored right away through the RPT Playground, which lets you run forecasts against built-in sample datasets or upload your own files. entry.title: How I Connected Claude Code to a Real SAP S/4HANA On-Premise System Using MCP
entry.content:
▶ Watch the full-quality video: https://youtu.be/8ZFwoMb9xrM

One prompt, one MCP tool call, 13 open maintenance notifications from an SAP S/4HANA on-premise test system, and a dashboard built from them.

I connected an AI agent to a real SAP S/4HANA on-premise system through the SAP Cloud Connector and an MCP server on SAP Integration Suite. No ABAP, no inbound firewall ports, no mock services in between: the agent reads maintenance notifications straight from the SAP system and then works with them.

The video above shows the agent turning those notifications into a dashboard. The same MCP server plugs into Claude Code with one command, so once real SAP objects are in a coding agent's context, it can write files, generate code and build things from them.

Scope, up front: this is a feasibility demo, not a production deployment. The backend is a real S/4HANA 2023 on-premise system, but it is a QA/test system loaded with test data I created for this scenario. Nothing here touches production, and the project continues in testing.

Part 3 of a series

Part 1 built the agent, Part 2 moved it to a governed gateway, Part 3 connects it to a real system.

This is Part 3 of my series on AI agents for SAP Plant Maintenance. In Part 1 I built the agent with CAP and Claude Desktop. In Part 2 I moved it to the governed MCP Gateway, but the data behind it was simulated by iFlows. This time there's an actual S/4HANA system on the other end.

What changed since Part 2: one box

Part 2 used simulated data. Part 3 adds a single new piece, the SAP Cloud Connector, and the agent reaches a real on-premise system.

The MCP side is almost the same as in Part 2. The MCP server runs on the Integration Cell of SAP Integration Suite and is generated from an API artifact, so I don't write or operate any server code. What's new is where the API points. It no longer points at a mock. It points at an on-premise S/4HANA, reached through the Cloud Connector.

If you haven't used the Cloud Connector before, think of it as a small agent installed on the SAP side of the network. It opens an outbound tunnel to SAP BTP, so nothing has to be opened inbound and the S/4HANA system is never exposed to the internet. SAP BTP can only reach the hosts and paths you explicitly allow, which in my case is one OData service.

How a question travels

Five hops, one outbound tunnel, real data back in a few seconds.

  1. You ask Claude Code something in plain language.
  2. The MCP server on SAP Integration Suite exposes the available tools, and Claude Code picks one.
  3. A governed API (OAuth, policies, monitoring) calls a BTP destination of type on-premise.
  4. The Cloud Connector carries the call through its tunnel into the network.
  5. SAP S/4HANA answers with the standard OData API for maintenance notifications (API_MAINTNOTIFICATION).

The round trip takes a few seconds. The agent only ever sees three read-only tools: list notifications, read one notification, and read its items.

Registering the server in Claude Code is a single command, because the same small stdio bridge from Part 2 handles the OAuth token:

claude mcp add sap-maintenance --scope user -- node bridge.js

From notifications to a dashboard

A chat answer is useful, but the real gain comes when the agent turns SAP data into something you can use. With the real notifications in context, it can write files, generate code and build pages from them.

I asked for a page with the open maintenance notifications of plant 1710, grouped by status and by equipment. The agent called the list tool, read the 13 open notifications from the test system, and built the dashboard:

The dashboard built from the 13 open notifications of plant 1710 in the test system.

13 open notifications: 5 with breakdown (M2) and 8 without (M1). All 13 are in status OSNO (outstanding), so the status view shows a single full bar. The agent kept NOPR, ORAS and NOCO on the chart with zero, to make it explicit that no notification is in those statuses instead of silently dropping them.

Clean core: what I changed in S/4HANA

  • Changed: activated one standard, SAP-released OData service (API_MAINTNOTIFICATION) in the Gateway.
  • Not changed: no ABAP, no custom objects, no inbound firewall ports, and no data replicated to SAP BTP (each call reads live from S/4HANA).

That matters beyond the demo. Agents reach SAP through a released API and a governed gateway, side by side with the core, which is the direction SAP recommends for third-party AI agents.

Three things that broke (so you don't lose the time I did)

  1. The API was created with no operations. Creating the API artifact from a destination left the OpenAPI spec empty. I pasted the spec in myself, with the three operations and their descriptions.
  2. Cloud Connector said "Not Reachable", but the server was up. The trace file showed the backend's TLS certificate had expired. On a test system, check certificates before you start debugging the network.
  3. My trial region wasn't in the Cloud Connector list. The trial runs on us10-001, and the right entry in the Cloud Connector is the main region host, cf.us10.

The agent stopped inventing

In Part 1 the agent got the data right but invented the meaning of a status code and built an answer on top of it. This time I put the meaning of the common statuses (open, in process, order assigned, completed) into the tool description, together with a plain rule: don't invent meanings for codes not on this list.

You can see it in the dashboard above: the status comes back from SAP as OSNO, and the agent reads it as outstanding because the tool description says so, not because it guessed.

MCP doesn't bring business context. The tool description does.

Honest limits

  • Test system, test data. It's a real S/4HANA 2023 on-premise QA system, but the notifications were created for this scenario. It's a feasibility demo, and it stays in testing.
  • About the video. It opens with a 5-second intro. After that, it shows the agent building the dashboard from the notifications in the test system.
  • Read-only, technical user. Every call reaches SAP with one technical identity. The next step for anything serious is principal propagation, so the SAP authorization of the person asking applies. This SAP post shows that path.
  • Trial tenant. Built on an SAP BTP trial. You can validate the pattern there before committing to a license.

If you're working on AI agents for SAP Plant Maintenance, EAM or asset management, let's talk in the comments or on LinkedIn.

Thanks for reading.

entry.title: Introducing Joule Studio Certification: Build real-world AI Skills. Practice. Prove What You Can Do.
entry.content:
We are proud to announce a brand new SAP Certification for developers and solution architects, building AI agents, applications, and workflows with Joule Studio, with one certification attempt available at no cost from September 30 through December 31, 2026.

AI is changing how software is built. And as development changes, so do the skills developers need to turn new ideas into solutions that work in the enterprise context.

For SAP developers and technical professionals, that increasingly means knowing how to move beyond understanding AI concepts to actually building with AI: creating agents, applications, and workflows, grounding them in business context, and managing them from development through deployment, and at scale.

SAP Certification is evolving alongside those skills.

This year marks 30 years of SAP Certification. Over three decades, certification has evolved alongside SAP technology, from the SAP R/3 era to today's cloud and AI-enabled enterprise landscape. Over the past year, that evolution has accelerated as SAP has reimagined certification around practical skills and how professionals actually work.

Now, we’re taking another leap forward with a new certification focused on agentic development.

From knowledge to practical skills

Over the past year, SAP has been reimagining its certification approach, shifting from traditional knowledge-based testing toward practical, performance-based assessments that reflect how professionals work. Rather than focusing on what learners can recall, the emphasis is now on demonstrating how they apply their skills to realistic challenges. The new Joule Studio Certification builds on this approach, validating the practical capabilities needed to develop AI agents, applications, and workflows.

Introducing Joule Studio Certification

Available now, the Joule Studio Developer Certification is a new SAP Certification for developers and technical professionals building and extending AI agents, applications, and workflows with Joule Studio, SAP’s AI-first development environment on the SAP Business AI Platform.

The certification provides a structured way to demonstrate practical proficiency with Joule Studio, from translating an idea into an agent to grounding that agent in SAP business context and managing its deployment and lifecycle.

It is designed for developers and technical professionals across the SAP ecosystem who want to demonstrate their ability to put AI development skills into practice.

What will the certification cover?

The Joule Studio Certification focuses on skills involved in taking AI development from idea to implementation.

These include:

  • Intent-based development: Translating a business idea into a deployable agent using Joule Studio’s natural-language-driven development experience.
  • Building and extending AI agents: Creating custom agents or extending LoB agents to address specific business needs.
  • Business context: Grounding agents in relevant SAP business data, processes, and context.
  • Deployment and lifecycle management: Managing, testing, and deploying agents and skills throughout their lifecycle.

Together, these capabilities reflect the broader value of Joule Studio: enabling developers to build AI agents, applications, and workflows grounded in business context, using development tools that fit their needs, with governance and security built in.

Most importantly, the certification is about demonstrating that these capabilities can be applied in practice.

Why practical validation matters for AI

AI development is moving quickly. New tools and capabilities continue to emerge, but knowing that a technology exists is very different from knowing how to use it effectively.

For developers, the real value comes from being able to take a business need and turn it into something useful: identifying the right approach, grounding AI in the appropriate context, building and extending capabilities, and managing what has been created.

That is why practical skills validation is an important part of SAP’s evolving certification approach.

As SAP advances its AI-first development strategy, certification can provide professionals with a way to demonstrate that they are not simply familiar with emerging technologies but can apply them to real development scenarios.

“For 30 years, SAP Certification has evolved alongside SAP technology and the professionals who use it. With Joule Studio Certification, we’re continuing that journey by giving developers a way to demonstrate the practical skills needed to build with AI. As AI becomes a bigger part of how solutions are developed, those skills will be critical to turning innovation into trusted solutions that deliver value in a business context.”

— Timo Schuette, Global Vice President, SAP Product & Solution Learning

Your Joule Studio Certification is on us

To give more developers and technical professionals across the SAP ecosystem an opportunity to build and validate these skills, one Joule Studio certification attempt is available at no cost from its launch in October through December 31, 2026.

Learners can claim a complimentary certification exam voucher through the SAP Learning site and use the available learning resources to prepare.

Ready to build your Joule Studio skills?

Start preparing, build your Joule Studio skills, and put them into practice.

Claim your free Joule Studio certification voucher

entry.title: Tired of Watching Claude? Make It Chirp.
entry.content:
The Problem

You're basically babysitting an AI If you use Claude Code for anything non-trivial like refactoring a module, generating test coverage, reworking a large prompt chain - you know the ritual. You kick off the task, switch windows, try to get other work done, then find yourself reflexively tabbing back every two minutes to check whether it's finished. It's the same anxiety loop as waiting for a CI pipeline, except the feedback loop is shorter and the temptation to check is even stronger.

Claude Code doesn't ship with a "notify me when done" button. So I built one.

What ClaudeChirp Does

ClaudeChirp is a pair of small shell scripts that plug into Claude Code's hook system. When a task finishes: A macOS Notification Center banner pops up - the title shows how long it ran and the body shows the first lines of Claude's own closing summary.

Optionally, a headless email lands in your Outlook inbox - no compose window, no focus steal, just a quiet message with the full summary and the duration. You configure a threshold (default: 5 minutes). Tasks shorter than the threshold are silently ignored.

You can also tell Claude per-task: "notify me when done" to force a notification, or "don't ping me" to suppress one.

How It Works

Claude Code supports lifecycle hooks, so shell commands that fire at key moments in a session:

UserPromptSubmit fires when you submit a prompt. ClaudeChirp uses this to record the current Unix timestamp for the session. Stop fires when Claude finishes a task. ClaudeChirp measures the elapsed time, extracts Claude's final message from the hook payload, and dispatches whichever notification channels are enabled. The Stop hook receives a JSON payload that includes the last assistants' message which is Claude's own summary of what it just did.

The email channel uses Outlook's AppleScript object model (tell application "Microsoft Outlook"), which is fully headless. No window opens, no focus changes, Outlook doesn't even come to the foreground. macOS prompts for Automation permission once on first run, and then it just works.

Six steps to set it up

Prerequisites: macOS, Claude Code, bash/python3/osascript (all pre-installed on macOS). Outlook only if you want the email channel.

  • git clone https://github.com/joshuasteinert/claudechirp
  • cd claudechirp
  • cp config.example ~/.claude/claudechirp/config
  • Edit config: set your email, threshold, and which channels to enable
  • ./install.sh

That's it. install.sh copies the hooks to ~/.claude/claudechirp/hooks and wires them into ~/.claude/settings.json. Restart Claude Code afterwards. Config file (~/.claude/claudechirp/config):

  • NOTIFY_EMAIL="" # required for mail channel
  • THRESHOLD_MINUTES=5 # only notify for tasks at least this long
  • NOTIFY_PING=1 # macOS Notification Center banner
  • NOTIFY_MAIL=1 # headless email via Outlook

You can use either channel independently so ping-only, mail-only, or both.

Verify it works

To verify whether the installation worked, you can set THRESHOLD_MINUTES to 0 and run any query in Claude Code. It should then send a ping or mail if enabled.

Try It

The project is on GitHub: https://github.tools.sap/I570066/ClaudeChirp.git

It's macOS-only for now (relies on osascript). It has no runtime dependencies beyond what ships with macOS. Install, configure, restart Claude Code and enjoy. If you use Claude Code for long-running tasks and find yourself switching back to check on it, this is the two-minute fix for that.

entry.title: Event-driven integration with SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh
entry.content:
When evaluating event-driven integration platforms, enterprises typically consider Apache Kafka (including Confluent), dedicated services on Azure, AWS or GCP, iPaaS vendors, or established messaging products from vendors such as TIBCO and IBM. No doubt all these technologies offer benefits for specific scenarios. But there is another option that should be part of the discussion: SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh is an enterprise-grade, multi-cloud, event-driven solution which forms part of SAP Integration Suite and offers differentiating capabilities that serve multiple scenarios in hybrid enterprise environments. This article discusses the key capabilities and how SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh fits into a broader integration architecture as well as its significance for Agentic AI.

What is an event mesh

An event mesh is a network of event brokers that routes messages between producers and consumers across distributed environments — cloud regions, separate geographies (including data sovereignty requirements), on-premises systems, third-party services and AI agents — without producers needing to know where consumers are or when they are available. This decoupling is a foundational property that distinguishes event-driven from request-reply (REST/SOAP) integration.

Event meshes are well suited to scenarios where:

  • State changes need to propagate in real time and consistently across multiple downstream consumers (e.g. order created gets sent simultaneously to inventory, finance, logistics, and customer notification systems)
  • Producers and consumers have different availability or scaling characteristics
  • Producers and consumers may be built using different technologies and protocols
  • You need reliable delivery with message ordering guarantees across distributed nodes and where node failures can be isolated for fault tolerance and graceful recovery
  • You want to integrate AI agents, microservices or SaaS applications quickly without building point-to-point API chains and with less disruption to existing operations

SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh — what it actually does

SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh is SAP's implementation of this pattern – a fully managed event broker service available as part of SAP Integration Suite. Key capabilities:

Protocol support

SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh supports AMQP, MQTT, JMS, REST (HTTP/S), and WebSocket. This matters because enterprise environments rarely standardize on one protocol — OT systems often speak MQTT, ERP integrations use AMQP or JMS, and web/mobile clients use REST or WebSocket. A broker that speaks all of these natively removes the translation layer.

Multi-cloud and hybrid deployment topology

You can deploy SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh event brokers across AWS, Azure, GCP, AliCloud and on-premises — and mesh them into a single logical event network. A message published on AWS can be consumed on-premises or on Azure without your producer knowing the consumer's location. Azure Event Grid or AWS EventBridge do not extend natively across cloud boundaries. This could be a consideration for enterprises that have hybrid landscapes and multiple cloud providers.

Dynamic message routing and topic filtering

SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh supports dynamic routing and topic-based filtering with wildcard subscriptions. Dynamic routing is a mechanism where brokers automatically share subscription information and route event messages to enable multi-cloud, multi-region, and hybrid event-driven architectures without custom middleware or routing logic. Topic filtering is a method where event consumers use hierarchical strings and wildcards to tell the broker which specific messages they want to receive. The broker matches published topics against consumer filters before sending the data. In addition to reducing network traffic and overhead, it has the important benefit that changing or adding a new consumer does not require reconfiguring event producers. This reduces coordination overhead and risk of disruption.

Part of SAP Integration Suite

SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh is included with SAP Integration Suite, enhanced edition and available as license option with other editions of SAP Integration Suite. It works with the other key capabilities of SAP Integration Suite: Cloud Integration (for message-based and API-led flows), and Edge Integration Cell (for private cloud and on-premises execution). Together, you have message-based, event-driven, and hybrid integration patterns all from a single, modern platform.

How SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh fits with Edge Integration Cell and Cloud Integration

These capabilities address different integration patterns, but together serving overall business process flows, from within a single platform:

  • Cloud Integration handles synchronous and asynchronous message-based flows — REST, SOAP, OData, EDI, and pre-built iFlows from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub (thousands of pre-built integration scenarios available)
  • Advanced event mesh handles asynchronous event-driven flows where decoupling, fan-out, and cross-cloud routing are required
  • Edge Integration Cell runs Cloud Integration flows on-premises or in a private cloud, for scenarios with data residency requirements or air-gapped environments

A concrete example: an S/4HANA business event (goods receipt posted) is published to SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh. SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh routes the event to multiple consumers in parallel — a warehouse management system on-premises (via Edge Integration Cell), a third-party logistics SaaS on AWS, and an analytics pipeline on Azure. The S/4HANA system publishes once; downstream systems consume independently. This fan-out pattern across a diverse technology landscape is a key strength of decoupled, asynchronous event-driven integration.

Beyond SAP landscapes

Advanced event mesh does not require SAP systems on either end. SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh is an event broker — producers and consumers can be any application that speaks AMQP, MQTT, JMS, or REST. Practical non-SAP use cases:

  • IoT device telemetry ingestion (MQTT from edge devices to cloud analytics)
  • Microservice event buses in Kubernetes environments
  • Cross-cloud event routing between Azure-native services and AWS workloads
  • Real-time notification and data exchange for end-to-end processes between business applications from other vendors or custom-built

If your architecture already runs SAP Integration Suite for SAP connectivity, then you can extend it to cover non-SAP event-driven patterns, consolidating under a single platform as opposed to requiring additional vendor solutions.

Significance for Agentic AI

As enterprises deploy AI agents that need to act on real-time business events – an order placed, an inventory threshold crossed, a process exception raised – the event mesh becomes the connectivity layer (“nervous system”) that makes agent coordination possible. Not only coordination but having up-to-date data and context to allow agents to make the best decisions.

SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh provides a managed, multi-protocol event backbone where business process events, as well as associated data and context, can be exchanged in real-time between AI agents, applications and data platforms – SAP and non-SAP.

By avoiding the request/reply (polling) nature of other integration approaches and combined with dynamic routing and topic filtering described above, message traffic is reduced because messages are only sent when a relevant business event occurs and only to the consumers that have subscribed to them. Extending this to Agentic AI, it means agents do not need to poll repeatedly and they can subscribe to exactly the events and messages relevant to them, as opposed to being activated for every message, which is potentially wasteful of LLM tokens. Further, the decoupled nature of event-driven integration means that introducing new consuming systems, including AI agents, can happen with less disruption to existing applications, systems and operations.

This positions SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh as a foundational component of SAP's Business AI platform strategy, not just an integration tool.

How SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh compares to common alternatives

Here is a comparison of event-driven capabilities across some common alternatives.

MuleSoft Anypoint

For event-driven integration, MuleSoft Anypoint MQ is an add-on service — it does not provide a native multi-cloud topology nor natively support open message-broker standards like AMQP, MQTT, or JMS for direct client connections. Instead, non-Mule applications must access queues and exchanges via REST APIs. Message routing and filtering is from defined rules that then assign messages to bound queues. Connectivity to SAP applications will require a MuleSoft application to bridge between. Whilst enterprises already using MuleSoft heavily may consider these as a workable path forwards, others looking to a greenfield event-driven architecture would need to evaluate against their requirements.

Azure Event Grid, Service Bus, Event Hubs and Storage Queues

Azure provides four event and messaging services with distinct use cases: Event Grid for reactive event routing within Azure; Service Bus for reliable enterprise transactional messaging; Event Hubs for high-throughput big data or telemetry ingestion; and Storage Queues for simple, cost-effective processing of large volumes of background messages. Each service has different protocols that are supported and that may mean you need more than one service to meet your enterprise requirements. Azure Event Grid and Service Bus support filtering server-side (before messages are sent to consumers). By design, Azure Event Hubs does not support filtering, instead relying on the consumer to inspect and then use or discard messages. Connectivity to SAP applications is primarily through the separate Azure Logic Apps service that includes an SAP connector, though other tooling and partner solutions are available. If your estate is predominantly Azure and not multi-cloud, this may be a sufficient option to evaluate.

Apache Kafka (including Confluent)

Kafka is a common choice for high-throughput, low-latency data streaming. But it can incur overhead proportional to the frequency that consumers poll topics stored on Kafka brokers, does not natively perform content-based routing, relies on consumers to handle topic filtering (wasting network bandwidth for discarded messages), lacks native multi-protocol support (like MQTT or AMQP), and can have high operational overhead when routing messages across multi-cloud environments, with wide area distribution often needing additional tools (e.g. Confluent Cluster Linking). Connectivity to SAP applications requires additional tooling, some available from SAP, some from specialized partner add-ons. If your primary use case is high-volume streaming at scale (clickstreams, sensor telemetry in the millions per second), Kafka is a choice to consider.

Getting started

Advanced event mesh is available as part of SAP Integration Suite, part of the SAP Business AI Platform. Relevant starting points:

  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub (hub.sap.com) — pre-built event-driven integration scenarios and event specifications for S/4HANA and other SAP products
  • SAP Integration Suite product page on sap.com — entitlement and service plan details
  • SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh documentation on help.sap.com — broker configuration, topic routing, and multi-cloud mesh setup
  • SAP Community — search 'Advanced Event Mesh' for implementation patterns and architecture discussions

In summary

If you are evaluating event-driven integration, whether that includes SAP business applications or not, then SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh deserves serious consideration alongside MuleSoft Anypoint MQ, Kafka and Azure’s event services. The key differentiators include multi-cloud mesh topology, breadth of supported protocols, plus dynamic routing and topic filtering. If you already use SAP Integration Suite, the operational consolidation is compelling — one platform, one vendor, one support path — compared to procuring and maintaining a separate event infrastructure.
