entry.title: Anomaly Detection with AI in SAP Cloud ALM for Operations
entry.content:
Introduction

Static thresholds are the weak spot of most monitoring setups. Set them too tight and operations teams drown in alerts. Set them too loose and a real problem slips through until a user calls the service desk. And a value that is perfectly normal on a Monday morning can be a warning sign on a Sunday night.

SAP Cloud ALM for Operations now addresses this with a set of AI capabilities that learn what "normal" looks like for your landscape and flag deviations from it. In this post I give an overview of these capabilities, explain how they fit together from detection to resolution, and share practical tips from customer projects on getting started.

What SAP Cloud ALM offers today

The AI capabilities are not a separate product. They are built into the existing monitoring use cases and fall into three groups: detecting anomalies, recommending thresholds, and helping to resolve alerts.

Use caseCapabilityWhat it does

Health Monitoring

Dynamic Thresholds

Calculates thresholds automatically from historical data and trend analysis, so the system learns the normal behavior of a metric and flags deviations.

Real User Monitoring

Change point detection and seasonal anomaly suppression

Detects significant changes in user-facing performance. Alerts caused by predictable patterns, such as weekly peaks or quarter-end spikes, can be suppressed.

Integration & Exception Monitoring

Anomaly detection on message volume

The event "Anomaly Detected in the Number of Messages Processed" fires when a business service processes more or fewer messages than expected within a time period.

Integration & Exception Monitoring

AI-recommended thresholds

Uses machine learning on historical message counts to suggest threshold values, shown with a trend chart of past volumes.

Business Process Monitoring

AI threshold recommendations

Analyzes the last seven days of document volumes and suggests KPI event thresholds for review.

Alert Management

ALM Alert Resolution Agent

Analyzes alert details, error messages, thresholds and system context, searches documentation, KBAs and SAP Notes, and suggests troubleshooting steps on the Alert Details page.

Dashboards

ALM Dashboard Generation Agent

Creates dashboard cards from system and service data using natural-language prompts.

 

In Health Monitoring, the Quality column shows how far each metric's model has come:

  • Predictive: the model is actively generating thresholds.
  • Learning: more data is being collected.
  • Static: the metric behaves too constantly for a reliable prediction.
  • Insufficient: there is not enough suitable data for predictive modeling.

SAP positions these features as steps toward "Autonomous ALM": from dynamic thresholds and change point detection today toward continuous detection of critical situations, guided resolution with Joule and, eventually, automated remediation.

How it works

 

The monitoring use cases collect the data, the AI layer learns what is normal and flags deviations, and Alert Management routes the result to the right team. The Alert Resolution Agent then supports the first analysis, so the team starts with context instead of a bare alert.

Getting started

The AI capabilities build on a working monitoring setup. If data is already flowing into SAP Cloud ALM, you can start in a few steps:

  1. Connect your systems and services. Anomaly detection needs history, so the earlier data collection starts, the sooner the models have something to learn from.
  2. Activate the monitoring use cases you want to use: Health Monitoring, Real User Monitoring, Integration & Exception Monitoring or Business Process Monitoring.
  3. Switch selected metrics to dynamic thresholds in Health Monitoring, and check the Quality column until they reach "Predictive".
  4. Use "Recommend" for anomaly events in Integration & Exception Monitoring. Review the suggested values against the trend chart, apply them, and regenerate them when the behavior of the monitored service changes.
  5. Accept or adjust the KPI threshold recommendations in Business Process Monitoring.
  6. Route the resulting alerts through Alert Management and Intelligent Event Processing to the right teams via email, Microsoft Teams or your ITSM tool.
  7. Use the ALM Alert Resolution Agent on the Alert Details page to speed up the first analysis.

Lessons from customer projects

  • Start where the noise is. Begin with the metrics and interfaces that generate the most false alerts today. That is where dynamic thresholds pay off fastest and win the trust of the operations team.
  • Give the models time. A metric in "Learning" or "Insufficient" state is not a configuration error. Keep static thresholds in place for critical metrics until the model is predictive.
  • Treat recommendations as a starting point. AI-recommended thresholds are based on past behavior. If the past contains an incident, review the values before you apply them.
  • Decide who gets which alert before go-live. Detection is only half the job. Agree with the Basis, integration and application teams which alerts go to whom and through which channel.
  • Mind the scope for non-SAP systems. Anomaly detection works on the data that reaches SAP Cloud ALM. Third-party systems need to be connected first, for example via OpenTelemetry.

entry.title: Building an ABAP AI Agent: From a Configuration Question to Live SAP Evidence
entry.content:
By @David150  and @Dinis_Shubin. We are students who built this S/4HANA prototype together.
A user asks why an S/4HANA configuration behaves a certain way. Before an agent can explain it, it must discover the relevant tables, understand their keys, and check the current settings. Our project tackles that investigation inside ABAP. For reusable agent memory, we chose Open Knowledge Format (OKF): a format that organizes readable knowledge into concepts, tags, links, and bundles. It lets us remember where to look and what a source means, so each question does not have to start the investigation from scratch.
 
The difficult part was making a language model useful in an older S/4HANA on-premise system. A model that can write a convincing answer is only the beginning. It also needs a working tool interface, evidence from SAP, and a loop that knows when to continue or stop. Even getting a newer model into that loop took changes we would not recommend for a production system.
 
What the SDK gives us, and what we built around it
The external model proposes investigation steps and ABAP executes them. Our agent class, Z_AGENT_V2, owns the conversation and the loop that alternates between model calls and tool execution. The classes and function modules with a Z_ prefix are our custom components.
 
The agent's constructor obtains a model client through the SDK factory call CL_AIC_ISLM_COMPL_API_FACTORY=>GET( )->CREATE_INSTANCE( 'Z_S4H_AGENTIC_SCEN' ). The returned client implements IF_AIC_COMPLETION_API, the SDK interface for submitting conversation messages to the model. Z_S4H_AGENTIC_SCEN is our Intelligent Scenario: the SAP configuration that selects the model connection. You can create such a scenario in the S/4 system via transaction F4469 and assign a model to it, in our case gpt-5.6-sol.
 
The SDK provides a message container for conversation history, function registration to tell the model which tools exist, and completion calls to request its next response. Our harness supplies the investigation loop, dispatch rules, execution checks, and knowledge maintenance. Our research-agent builder, Z_RESEARCH_AGENT_BUILDER, assembles five capabilities: executing generated ABAP, listing OKF bundles, opening a bundle directory, searching concepts, and reading a concept. The tool class, Z_TOOLS_V2, supplies their descriptions and parameter definitions. The agent's REGISTER_TOOL method converts those definitions into SDK function schemas, using ABAP runtime type information to describe parameter types.
 
 

The WebSocket worker retains a controller, which builds the research agent and starts a separate agent to maintain knowledge after each answer. The conversation post explains how that worker keeps context available across turns.

 

The agent's main method, PERFORM_AGENT_INTERACTION, submits the current conversation with the SDK's EXECUTE_FOR_MESSAGES. The returned response exposes the model's requested actions through GET_TOOL_CALLS. Before executing an action, the agent checks its name against the registered tool catalog. It attaches the execution result to that tool call with SET_CALL_RESULT, then appends the calls and their results to the conversation using ADD_TOOL_RESULTS. The next model call therefore receives the evidence needed to decide whether to investigate further. A response without tool calls ends the normal loop.
 
This is the moment a chat becomes an investigation: the next question can depend on what SAP actually returned.
 
From generated code to an answer the model can inspect
Consider a question about a configuration assignment. The agent might first inspect SAP Dictionary metadata to discover the table's fields and keys, then issue a focused query using them. It supplies the body of an existing ABAP subroutine, declared with FORM, and must assign its result to a predefined string variable named output. That string becomes the tool response the model can inspect.

Our execution tool, Z_TOOLS_V2->EXECUTE_CODE_IN_S4, first delegates validation to the custom scanner class Z_DYNAMIC_CODE_SCANNER. Its CHECK_IF_CODE_IS_SAFE method uses the standard SCAN ABAP-SOURCE statement to inspect the generated statements and reject database writes, locking reads, and unapproved calls. Restricted execution is enabled by default. SELECT SINGLE is permitted because it returns at most one row while other SELECT queries need a literal row limit from 1 to 1,000. This filters generated operations. It does not replace business data authorization or workload controls.

Our wrapper function module, Z_EXECUTE_GENERATED_CODE, puts accepted source inside that subroutine and calls the compilation-and-execution helper Z_GEN_EXEC_SUBROUTINE synchronously with DESTINATION 'NONE'. This is a local Remote Function Call (RFC): execution stays in the same SAP system but runs in a separate ABAP session. The helper uses GENERATE SUBROUTINE POOL to compile the source into a temporary ABAP program containing the subroutine, then executes it. Compilation errors and caught runtime exceptions return as tool feedback, giving the model a chance to correct its attempt.

We switched to this RFC approach after first hitting ABAP's limit on the number of generated subroutine pools in one internal session. Repeated execution of LLM-generated code had exhausted that session's allowance. After each execution, Z_EXECUTE_GENERATED_CODE calls RFC_CONNECTION_CLOSE for destination NONE, so the next generated snippet runs in a fresh ABAP internal session with its own subroutine-pool allowance. The synchronous call lets the agent wait for the result while keeping those generated pools out of its retained conversation session.
 

 A failed query can supply useful feedback. The harness returns diagnostics instead of silently losing the investigation step.

 
A loop-counter cap of 25 triggers a forced completion call requesting a final answer. Our conversation coordinator, Z_AGENT_CONTROLLER, is retained by the WebSocket worker and keeps the research agent across turns. After an answer, it hands that turn's evidence to the asynchronous function module Z_OKF_WRITE_TURN_ASYNC. Our writer builder, Z_OKF_WRITE_AGENT_BUILDER, creates a fresh agent for that background task, with tools for maintaining OKF and the same restricted execution tool for verifying findings. This gives answering questions and curating reusable knowledge separate objectives.

The model upgrade that crossed into SAP standard objects

Our S/4HANA system did not include the newer models we wanted to try. We manually added model entries to the ISLM tables ISLM_PRV_MDL and ISLM_PRV_MDLVRSN. Registration alone was insufficient: the permitted models were also hardcoded in AIC_MODEL_ID and CL_AIC_LLM_MAP_FACT_PROV, so we modified those SAP SDK objects too.

We do not recommend this approach. It changes SAP standard table content and SAP standard code, and updates can overwrite or conflict with those changes. We accepted that tradeoff for our prototype. It is not a production recommendation or a supported extension mechanism.

There was a second boundary we could not solve by adding model IDs. The ABAP AI SDK version in our system uses OpenAI's Chat Completions API, rather than the newer Responses API. With our selected model we could not adjust the reasoning settings or temperature as intended.

The endpoint also limits future upgrades. For example, gpt-6.1-sol requires the Responses API for tool calls (see the official OpenAI model overview ). Until the ABAP SDK supports that endpoint, models with this requirement cannot power this agent through the SDK. Without tool calls, the model cannot request the SAP investigation steps on which the agent depends. A successful model registration would therefore still leave the essential capability missing.

What we would like the SDK to handle next

We would like the SDK to support token streaming and tool calls together. In the SDK version we use, token streaming is available only without tool calls. Our agent needs tool calls to investigate SAP, so it uses the synchronous EXECUTE_FOR_MESSAGES method and waits for each model response to finish. We send tool-progress events during the investigation, but deliver the final answer as a complete response. Streaming text as the model generates it while also supporting tool calls would let readers start seeing the answer sooner without giving up the agent's investigation capabilities.

Conversation compaction (summarizing older history to keep the model's working context manageable) was another responsibility we had to implement ourselves. Our agent keeps the SDK message container, messages, alongside its own ordered history, messages_cp, and the tool-call objects in tool_calls. Those parallel records let us reconstruct the conversation after a summary replaces older turns. The agent's COMPACT_CONTEXT method creates that summary. Our utility method Z_AGENT_UTIL=>BUILD_MESSAGE_CONTAINER rebuilds the SDK container with the retained messages and tool results. Keeping these representations aligned adds application work that we would like the SDK to reduce with automatic compaction methods.

The result is an ABAP harness whose decisions are inspectable: registered tools, checked execution, returned evidence, and explicit memory handling. The next posts look at two questions that became just as important as the model call: what the agent should remember in OKF, and how a follow up reaches the same conversation.

entry.title: Agent Memory in S/4HANA: Why We Store Open Knowledge Format in Z Tables
entry.content:
By @David150  and @Dinis_Shubin. We are students who built this S/4HANA prototype together.

Two users ask similar questions about an S/4HANA configuration. Without reusable system memory, the agent may repeat the same broad ABAP searches: finding candidate tables, inspecting their keys, and rediscovering what their fields mean. We wanted each investigation to give the next one a better starting point. We chose Open Knowledge Format (OKF) because it organizes readable concept documents with metadata, tags, and explicit links into a persistent map of the system.

Every new user question is an opportunity for the agent to learn more about this particular SAP system. Verified discoveries can become shared OKF knowledge: which tables or objects matter, how they connect, and how to interpret them. When a similar question arrives, that map directs the agent to the relevant sources. Once OKF provides a sufficient mapping, the agent can skip the broad discovery search and perform a focused live read instead.

The more difficult question came next: what should the agent remember? Saving a current configuration value could make tomorrow's answer stale. Saving only a chat transcript could bury the useful discovery in pages of tool output. Our working rule is to remember source locations, keys, relationships, and meanings, then read actual settings and business results live. Learning here means growing and correcting that reusable system map as questions reveal new evidence.

OKF, explained through a SAP investigation

An OKF concept describes one asset or meaning in a Markdown document with YAML metadata. Concepts belong to bundles, which provide a collection and navigation directory. Tags classify concepts; links describe relationships between them. The format defines how knowledge is represented and exchanged, without requiring a particular database or runtime.

Consider an illustrative question about a configuration assignment for one organizational unit. The first investigation may need broad SAP Dictionary searches to find the source table, identify the organizational key, and establish the assignment's meaning. One OKF concept can preserve the table and key information; another can explain the business meaning. A link connects them, and a domain tag makes them easier to find.

A later question about the same kind of assignment for another organizational unit can reuse that mapping. The agent loads the relevant concept, uses the documented key to target the source table, and reads the requested unit's current assignment. The earlier discovery has become useful beyond the question that produced it. If the map lacks a needed source or relationship, the agent investigates that gap and can retain the new finding for future questions.

Our agent instructions make this concrete: consult OKF before source discovery, load a known relevant concept directly when possible, and stop exploring once the mapping is sufficient. Otherwise, search for relevant concepts first, using concise keywords, and follow the relationships needed for the question.

Avoiding context clutter is crucial as OKF grows. A bundle's Markdown index can become quite large. Loading it routinely would fill the model's working context with navigation entries unrelated to the question, consuming space needed for relevant evidence and the conversation. That is why we instruct the agent to use targeted concept search before opening the bundle index. The index is a fallback when searches and selected concept reads leave a specific navigation gap. A growing system map should make retrieval more focused, rather than introduce another broad read into every investigation.

Four tables make the memory concrete

The ZOKF_* tables and Z-prefixed ABAP components named below are custom parts of our prototype. Their roles explain how the memory works, independently of the particular class names. We store the graph in four transparent database tables, each keyed by SAP client so that clients have separate knowledge records:

Table What it holds
ZOKF_BUNDLEBundle metadata, the Markdown directory in index_md, format version, and changed_at revision.
ZOKF_CONCEPTConcept identity, type, title, description, Markdown body in body_md, lifecycle status, and timestamps.
ZOKF_TAGOne classification per bundle/concept/tag association.
ZOKF_LINKDirected source-to-target relationships with readable link_text.
 

 

The Markdown body explains the finding. Separate tag and link rows make it searchable and connected without parsing every document.

Our knowledge-service class, Z_OKF_CONCEPT_SERVICE, is the ABAP access layer for this graph. Its LIST_BUNDLES method returns the available collections, SEARCH_CONCEPTS finds relevant concept summaries, and GET_CONCEPT loads a selected document with its incoming and outgoing links. GET_BUNDLE_INDEX opens the bundle's Markdown navigation directory when targeted searches and concept reads leave a navigation gap. Our tool class, Z_TOOLS_V2, exposes these operations as functions the model can request during an investigation.

Search can filter by literal keywords, concept type, tag, hierarchy prefix, and lifecycle status. A hierarchy prefix selects concepts in a particular branch of their path-like identifiers. The search tool returns a bounded page of compact summaries and a continuation cursor for the next page.

Pagination prevents search results from cluttering the model's context. Even a targeted search can match many concepts as the map grows. Returning all matches at once would consume context space with material the agent may never need, leaving less room for relevant evidence and the conversation. The agent requests another page only when it needs more relevant candidates, keeps the search filters unchanged between pages, and stops once it has a sufficient mapping. It then loads the selected concept bodies rather than bringing the entire result set into context.

The table keys make identities explicit: a concept is identified by client, bundle, and its path-like concept_id. This is a graph implemented with ordinary relational records, close to the SAP sources it describes.

Writing memory is a separate investigation

Our conversation coordinator, Z_AGENT_CONTROLLER, separates answering from knowledge maintenance. After a completed turn, it hands the question, answer, and tool evidence to the asynchronous function module Z_OKF_WRITE_TURN_ASYNC. That background task uses our writer builder, Z_OKF_WRITE_AGENT_BUILDER, to create a fresh agent whose job is to review and maintain the system map.

The writer's policy comes from our prompt-provider class through Z_PROMPTS=>GET_OKF_WRITER_SYSTEM_PROMPT. It requires direct, current, read-only evidence for material facts and a search for existing concepts before creating duplicates. Verification code passes through our source scanner, Z_DYNAMIC_CODE_SCANNER, which rejects writes and unapproved operations before generated ABAP executes.

This review turns a question into a chance to improve shared memory. The writer can add a missing source, clarify a key, or correct an existing relationship. A reusable finding should identify the source, keys, and interpretation that another investigation can verify. A turn that reveals no new or corrected durable knowledge needs no write; learning accumulates through verified discoveries rather than by saving every answer.

Our WebSocket entry path uses this coordinator too. Its retained conversation worker, ZDS_CONVERSATION_WORKER, creates one Z_AGENT_CONTROLLER, whose constructor obtains the investigation agent, Z_AGENT_V2, from Z_RESEARCH_AGENT_BUILDER. The builder registers SAP investigation and read-only OKF navigation tools. Each turn goes through the controller, which starts the separate background writer after the investigation completes. OKF maintenance tools belong to that writer's catalog.

The hard part: two writers can learn at once

Suppose two asynchronous writers read the same bundle directory. One adds a concept; the other updates a relationship. If both simply save their original directory plus their own edit, the later save could erase the earlier discovery. Agent memory needs a concurrency contract as much as it needs readable documents.

Our tool class, Z_TOOLS_V2, stages proposed concept, tag, link, bundle, and directory changes in memory. These proposals have not yet changed the database. Its FINALIZE_OKF_CHANGES method submits them together to the knowledge service's APPLY_CHANGE_SET method, which validates and persists the complete change, then the tool clears staging. The service checks SAP's S_TABU_NAM table-access authorization object and validates the inputs before locking affected records and preparing the rows to write.

Each proposal includes expected_changed_at, the bundle revision timestamp the writer originally read. The service's LOAD_LOCKED_STATE method acquires database locks and loads the records needed to assess the proposal. It processes bundle IDs in a consistent sorted order and uses a conditional UPDATE on ZOKF_BUNDLE to lock only the expected revision. If another writer has changed the bundle, finalization returns a “reload and restage” error. The writer must reread the current knowledge, reassess its complete proposal, and submit it again.

 

 The concept, its tags and links, and the navigation directory cross one commit boundary together.

Successful persistence ends with COMMIT WORK AND WAIT, making all prepared database changes durable together. Failures in the database phase lead to ROLLBACK WORK, undoing changes from that transaction. This avoids a half-updated graph in which a directory points to a concept that was never saved. The protection relies on writers using the service protocol consistently.

Useful memory still needs limits

Concepts can be draft, stable, or deprecated: knowledge being prepared, knowledge available for normal use, or knowledge retained for history. Search defaults to stable concepts. Verification is recorded separately in the verified_at timestamp for explicit concept changes during finalization. That timestamp records the writer's assertion of verification; it does not expire automatically or guarantee that the source remains correct.

Deprecation preserves a concept for historical navigation. The writer can link a replacement, remove misleading tags or links, and adjust the directory in one change set. Direct retrieval still exposes the deprecated concept and its status.

Our representation implements a focused subset of OKF 0.2. Portable bundle export, multiple verifier identities, and per-run computation attestation are outside the current implementation. Custom Z-table storage is the working representation; it is not yet a complete OKF import/export pipeline.

There is also a second kind of memory: the current conversation. We had to build our own compaction around the ABAP AI SDK, maintaining a custom history alongside its message container. Compaction preserves the working context of a chat; OKF preserves curated knowledge for later investigations. The conversation post explains the implementation and why we would like the SDK to provide more of this machinery.

The exciting part is that a user question can leave the agent better equipped for the next one. As verified discoveries accumulate, similar investigations can go straight to the needed tables, views, and objects instead of repeating broad ABAP searches. The system map grows with use, while current values still come from live SAP reads. That is the learning we wanted OKF to make possible.

entry.title: Keeping an ABAP AI Conversation Alive: WebSockets, Follow-Ups, and Compaction
entry.content:
By @David150  and @Dinis_Shubin  — students building this S/4HANA prototype together.

“Which assignments did you check?” is a simple follow-up, but an agent cannot answer it reliably if every request creates a fresh conversation. We needed to keep the question, tool evidence, and previous answer available across turns while delivering progress to the browser. Our project also uses Open Knowledge Format (OKF), which organizes readable concepts, tags, links, and bundles into reusable memory. OKF suits discoveries that should survive a chat; this post tackles the immediate conversation context that makes a follow-up meaningful.

We also faced a visibility problem: while the agent was investigating, users had no way to tell what state it was in or what it was currently doing. We introduced the WebSocket connection to stream all agent events, including tool calls, tool results, context compaction, and the final response. Users can therefore follow the investigation as it progresses, see which tool is being called, and see its results as they arrive.

The browser transcript looked like an obvious place to start. The state the model actually receives, however, lives in an ABAP object: the SDK message container, which holds the instructions and conversation messages submitted to the model. Keeping it available while synchronous model calls run led us to three responsibilities: a handler that receives questions, a worker that retains and runs the agent, and a relay that delivers events independently of that execution. The Z-prefixed classes and function modules below are our custom components; SAP supplies the channel frameworks and SDK interfaces they use.

The first obstacle was getting connected

Setting up the ABAP WebSocket connection to our S/4HANA system took several hours. ABAP Push Channels (APC) expose the WebSocket endpoint; ABAP Messaging Channels (AMC) carry messages between our ABAP sessions. We configured the APC application in transaction SAPC, its Internet Communication Framework (ICF) service in SICF, and the internal messaging channels in SAMC. Activating an ABAP class was only one part of making the endpoint usable.

Our WebSocket handler class, ZDS_PROMPT_STREAM_WS, is the SAP-side entry point for incoming connections and prompts. It inherits from SAP's CL_APC_WS_EXT_STATELESS_BASE, the framework base class for a stateless plain WebSocket handler. The IF_APC_WS_EXTENSION interface defines callbacks that SAP invokes when a connection opens, a message arrives, or the connection closes. We handle those notifications here and keep conversation memory in the worker.

The similarly named CL_APC_WSP_EXT_STATELESS_BASE supports the WebSocket Push Channel Protocol variant, a different connection type. Selecting the existing plain WebSocket handler class in SAPC, configuring its service, and aligning channel access and filter names all mattered.

For example, a channel binding connects outgoing messages to the WebSocket for a particular request. Both that binding and our event publisher use a CORRELATION_ID filter to select the request's messages. Different filter names on the sending and receiving sides will not form the intended route. These details turned “connect a WebSocket” into a SAP integration task rather than a single networking call.

One question gets one identity

The application backend sends a JSON text frame over WebSocket Secure (WSS):

{ "type": "prompt", "prompt": "Which assignments did you check?" }

The WebSocket handler validates the prompt, reserves the connection's single active request, and returns an accepted frame with a fresh correlation_id. This confirms that SAP has admitted the question for processing; it does not mean the model has answered it. Progress follows. An illustrative successful terminal answer looks like this:

{
  "outcome": "ok",
  "response_type": "final_response",
  "is_final": true,
  "correlation_id": "0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF",
  "step": 3,
  "content": "The complete answer."
}
Field Meaning
outcomeaccepted admits the request, progress carries intermediate events, and ok completes a successful answer.
response_typeIdentifies tool_call, tool_response, context_compaction, or final_response.
is_finalEnds the request when true. The protocol also permits non-terminal answer chunks.
correlation_idIdentifies one request and its replay records. Each question gets a new ID.
stepOrders public events within that request, rather than counting model iterations or tokens.

The application backend bridges the browser and SAP. It keeps tool details separate from answer text and translates SAP events into browser server-sent events (SSE), including answer-delta for answer content and complete for request completion. SSE delivers updates over an HTTP connection from the backend to the browser. The backend holds the SAP WebSocket and credentials.

 

A request crosses two transports and several ABAP sessions. Its correlation ID ties the public events together.

Why one ABAP session was not enough

A synchronous SDK completion or tool call occupies the worker's execution path until it returns. Delivery needs its own session to receive and forward progress during that time. Our background function module, ZDS_PROMPT_STREAM_BG, coordinates delivery for one request: it creates a relay, subscribes it to the request's events, and only then starts the worker or sends it a follow-up. That ordering gives even a fast event a receiver waiting for it. The WebSocket handler establishes the outgoing channel binding, launches this asynchronous processing, and returns from its message callback.

The agent sends AMC events as Push Channel Protocol (PCP) messages, whose named fields carry the request ID, event type, content, and finality. Our relay class, ZDS_LLM_RESPONSE_RELAY, receives those events and holds them in a queue. Its START_DELIVERY method subscribes to the channel; SAP then invokes its receiver callback when a message arrives.

The callback only queues the event. After the standard WAIT FOR MESSAGING CHANNELS statement returns control to the background task, that task repeatedly calls the relay's PROCESS_NEXT_EVENT method to drain the queue and pass events to the publisher. This separation matters because saving output requires COMMIT WORK, the ABAP transaction commit statement, which cannot run inside that receiver callback.

Our output-publisher class, ZDS_PROMPT_STREAM_PUBLISHER, turns a validated internal event into the public JSON frame. It assigns the frame's step number, saves and commits it for replay, then sends the JSON through request-filtered AMC text to the WebSocket binding. The relay receives and queues; the publisher validates, stores, and sends. Persisting before notification means the event is available for replay before a live client receives it.

The follow-up must reach the same owner

Our conversation-worker class, ZDS_CONVERSATION_WORKER, provides the lifetime that the stateless WebSocket handler does not. It runs in a long-lived ABAP internal session started by an asynchronous Remote Function Call (RFC). Its RUN method creates one Z_AGENT_CONTROLLER, processes the first question, and waits for later commands instead of ending after the first answer.

The controller's constructor obtains Z_AGENT_V2, our class for the model-and-tool investigation loop, from Z_RESEARCH_AGENT_BUILDER. On each turn, the worker invokes the controller's PERFORM_AGENT_INTERACTION method with the new prompt, request ID, and worker key. The controller delegates to the same research agent, whose conversation history remains available for the next question, and then starts a separate asynchronous OKF writer with the completed turn's evidence.

Our session-registry class, ZDS_CONVERSATION_SESSION_STORE, tracks which live connection belongs to which worker and whether a turn is active. It resolves the original WebSocket handshake's Sec-WebSocket-Key header to a private worker key and independently checks the SAP user and client. The worker key identifies the conversation owner across requests; the correlation ID identifies only one question.

The registry uses our database table ZDS_CON_SESSION for ownership and lifecycle metadata, such as whether a worker is ready or processing a turn. The live agent and its message history remain in the worker's memory. A routing key therefore does not replace the ownership checks or restore the agent by itself.

Inside the agent, the messages field references an SDK object implementing IF_AIC_MESSAGE_CONTAINER, the interface for building conversation history. The constructor sets the system role—the instructions that guide the agent. Each interaction appends the user's question, tool results, and assistant answer. The SDK's EXECUTE_FOR_MESSAGES method submits that container to the model, including the evidence the follow-up refers to.

 

Request relays change from turn to turn. Conversation state stays with the worker while it remains alive.

A later prompt uses the same physical SAP WebSocket, a new correlation ID, and a new output binding. Our command-publisher class, ZDS_CON_COMMAND_PUBLISHER, uses its SEND_TURN method to send that prompt and request ID to the existing worker over a private AMC command channel. A WORKER_KEY filter selects the worker that owns the conversation, while CORRELATION_ID filters scope the outgoing events to this particular request.

Overlapping requests are rejected before they can replace the active binding. The backend's application conversation ID selects its SAP socket; SAP routes the prompts using its own connection and worker registry.

When the history outgrows the container

Compaction summarizes older conversation history so it can continue to fit within the model's working context. The SDK version we used did not provide the automatic compaction methods we wanted, so we implemented the agent's COMPACT_CONTEXT method ourselves.

Alongside the SDK container, we continuously maintain messages_cp, our ordered copy of the conversation, using the SDK message-table type IF_AIC_MESSAGE_CONTAINER_INT=>MESSAGES. We also retain the actual tool-call objects in tool_calls. The custom history records message order and content; the tool objects preserve the calls and results needed to rebuild an SDK conversation.

The current trigger compares recorded token usage with 80% of context_window, our hardcoded context-budget constant of 1,000,000. These are prototype configuration choices, rather than a discovered limit for every deployed model. When enough older history exists, COMPACT_CONTEXT keeps the latest three user turns and asks the model to summarize the preceding history.

Our prompt provider class, Z_PROMPTS, supplies the summarization instructions through its GET_COMPACTION_PROMPT method. The agent inserts the resulting summary after the system instructions. Our utility class, Z_AGENT_UTIL, then uses its BUILD_MESSAGE_CONTAINER method to replay the retained messages, media, and tool results into a fresh SDK container. These helpers provide the summary policy and reconstruction work; the retained agent coordinates the operation.

Rebuilding must preserve message ordering, tool-result associations, and retained media. A summary alone cannot reconstruct those SDK objects. Keeping the SDK container and our custom representation aligned became additional application work. We would like the ABAP AI SDK to take more of that work off developers' shoulders with methods for automatic compaction.

The agent emits context_compaction progress events around this step. The retained agent survives, but its SDK container can be replaced. Continuity depends on the context carried forward, rather than permanent identity of the original container. OKF complements this by storing curated source knowledge beyond the worker's lifetime.

A live socket and a remembered conversation have different lifetimes

Browser SSE can reconnect while the backend's SAP socket stays live. Replacing the SAP WebSocket is different: SAP can replay one request's output by correlation ID, but future prompts on the replacement socket start fresh context. Replay may duplicate steps, so clients must deduplicate by correlation ID and step. The current backend reports upstream conversation loss instead of automatically using SAP replay.

Worker memory expires after approximately 15 idle minutes. Keepalive pings preserve connectivity; they do not count as conversation turns. The WebSocket handler's current close callback leaves worker cleanup to idle expiry. A restored browser transcript therefore does not establish restored ABAP memory.

There is a similar distinction in streaming. The protocol permits answer chunks, but the SDK version we use supports token streaming only without tool calls. Our agent needs those calls to investigate SAP, so it uses EXECUTE_FOR_MESSAGES synchronously and emits the completed answer as one terminal event. Tool progress can arrive earlier; answer text is delivered once the model response is complete. If a user stops waiting after SAP receives a prompt, the backend still drains the request to its terminal event to preserve socket ordering.

For this SDK integration, newer model capabilities also depend on endpoint support. As explained in the harness post, our ABAP SDK uses Chat Completions. Models such as gpt-6.1-sol require the Responses API for tool calls; the official OpenAI model reference documents that requirement. Keeping conversation state alive cannot compensate for a missing tool-calling interface.

The follow-up question now has a concrete path to its evidence: a fresh request reaches the retained worker and controller, which reuse the research agent's earlier investigation. That agent has SAP investigation and read-only OKF navigation tools. The controller hands completed-turn evidence to a separate background writer with OKF maintenance tools, while the research agent retains the conversation memory described here.

entry.title: Can You Run a Space Station? Lessons on Sustainability from the Dubai Museum of the Future
entry.content:
The Metaphor of the Orbiting Outpost
If you step onto Level 2 of the Dubai Museum of the Future, you will encounter the OSS Hope Simulator from SAP. Set against a glowing, interactive console, it presents users with a direct challenge: "Can you run a space station?"
 
To enterprise architects, developers, and consultants, this installation is far more than a visionary gaming experience. A space station operates as a strictly closed system. There is no margin for error; every drop of water, molecule of carbon, and unit of energy must be meticulously logged, tracked, and reused.
This setup mirrors our situation on Earth. Our planet is a closed ecosystem facing finite resource boundaries. The exhibit emphasizes that the exact same real-time data tracking required to sustain life in space is essential to preserving our enterprise ecosystems on Earth.
 
The Three Pillars of a Circular Enterprise
The logic of the simulator relies on keeping three core metrics balanced. These variables map directly to SAP's foundational sustainability pillars:
  • Zero Emissions: Moving beyond simple carbon estimation to active, automated decarbonization across the entire supply chain.
  • Zero Waste: Shifting production models from linear consumption to fully circular material loops where nothing is discarded.
  • Zero Inequalities: Establishing transparent workforce safety, ethical sourcing, and corporate governance down to the last tier of suppliers.
In a space station, you cannot survive without a central ledger to balance these vectors. On Earth, you cannot optimize what you do not accurately count.
 
️ Decoding the Architecture behind the "Wall of Knowledge"
The installation features an interactive "Wall of Knowledge" that showcases real-world global use cases. The simulator's backend logic runs on eight distinct technology domains. Five of these domains form the core foundation of the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) ecosystem:
 
1. Embedded AI & Predictive Forecasting
  • Simulation Mechanics: Dynamically balancing oxygen reserves and predicting machinery failure points before they occur.
  • SAP Enterprise Deployment: Embedding native intelligence via SAP Business AI and SAP Joule to flag supply chain anomalies, forecast emissions spikes, and automate ledger corrections before period-end close.
2. Advanced Real-Time Analytics
  • Simulation Mechanics: Aggregating and visualizing live telemetry across life support, energy grids, and cargo bays.
  • SAP Enterprise Deployment: Ingesting highly disparate IoT and operational data into the high-speed data tier of SAP HANA. This feeds directly into an auditable ESG reporting layer via the SAP Sustainability Control Tower.
 
3. Digital Twins & Simulation Sandboxes
  • Simulation Mechanics: Testing the operational risk of environmental adjustments inside a safe virtual environment first.
  • SAP Enterprise Deployment: Mapping asset management data to live logistics feeds. This allows operations leads to simulate structural facility changes before committing physical resources.
4. Blockchain & Asset Traceability
  • Simulation Mechanics: Verifying the origin, safety, and operational lifecycle of all arriving raw materials.
  • SAP Enterprise Deployment: Utilizing immutable ledger records to verify end-to-end supply chain transparency, ensuring strict compliance with evolving international sustainability regulations.
5. Hyper-Automation
  • Simulation Mechanics: Executing real-time automated adjustments to life support loops to completely eliminate human delay.
  • SAP Enterprise Deployment: Orchestrating touchless business workflows across SAP S/4HANA to dynamically adjust production rates based on resource availability.
The Enterprise Lesson: Profit and Planet on a Single Platform
The ultimate takeaway for the SAP ecosystem is clear: the precision engineering needed to pilot a space station matches the exact methodology required to run a sustainable business.
As technology professionals, the configurations, custom code lines, and system integrations we build on SAP BTP serve as the actual plumbing for global resource consumption. By integrating carbon, waste, and social ledgers directly into our core ERP data structures, we turn abstract sustainability goals into repeatable, daily business operations.

entry.title: How to Integrate an AI Assistant into an SAP Transaction Using ABAP AI tools
entry.content:
How to Integrate an AI Assistant into an SAP Transaction Using ABAP AI tools

 

 

 

 

 

 

Here, we will walk through a step-by-step implementation of an AI Assistant in the BP transaction using ABAP AI tools, along with the building blocks required for this integration.

We will use the BP transaction because it is available in SAP ABAP trial systems. This makes the example useful for ABAP developers who use trial systems to learn and experiment.

General Technical Prerequisites

As with any custom development within a standard SAP transaction, integrating an AI Assistant requires an appropriate enhancement or extension mechanism, such as a BAdI, a user exit, or another supported enhancement option.

Ideally, users should be able to open the AI Assistant on demand. To achieve this, the SAP transaction must provide a way to customize its user interface, allowing us to add an entry point for the Assistant. This could be a menu option, a screen element, or another interactive UI component, depending on the extension options available in the transaction.

Some SAP transactions provide specific mechanisms for customizing or extending their user interfaces. The BP transaction is a good example, as it uses the Business Data Toolset (BDT), a central framework for configuring and extending Business Partner (BP) maintenance screens, dialog programs, and transactions without modifying standard SAP source code.

Other standard transactions may not provide a supported way to add custom menus or screen elements. In such cases, it may still be possible to open the AI Assistant automatically when the transaction starts. To achieve this, we need to identify an appropriate enhancement option, such as a BAdI or user exit, that is triggered at a suitable point during the transaction's execution and allows the Assistant to be launched.

The key takeaway is that we need to analyze each standard transaction to determine the available options for integrating the AI Assistant, whether through a user interface enhancement or an alternative mechanism.

ABAP AI tools Prerequisites

This example requires both ABAP AI tools and ABAP AI tools User Interface to be installed on your system.

For the ABAP AI tools installation, see: https://github.com/christianjianelli/yaai

For the ABAP AI tools User Interface installation, see: https://github.com/christianjianelli/yaai_ui

The Business Partner AI Assistant

For the AI Assistant's user interface, we will use the ABAP AI tools User Interface to provide the chat interface through which users can interact with the Assistant.

To implement the AI Assistant itself, we will use ABAP AI tools, providing system instructions and tools.

Extending the Business Partner Transaction

For this example, we are going to configure a custom event that will be available in the Extras → More Extras menu in the BP transaction. We will use this custom event to provide users with a way to open the AI Assistant chat.

The steps are as follows:

1. Create a function group, for example, ZFG_AAI_BP.

2. In this function group, create a function module with the same parameters as the standard function module BUA_BUPA_EVENT_FCODE. For example, Z_F_EVENT_FCODE_YAAI. The function code YAAI will be used to instantiate the AI Assistant chat.

FUNCTION Z_F_EVENT_FCODE_YAAI
  IMPORTING
    VALUE(I_FCODE) LIKE TBZ4-FCODE OPTIONAL
    VALUE(I_CRSFIELD) LIKE BUS000TBFL-TBFLD OPTIONAL
    VALUE(I_CRSLINE) LIKE SY-LILLI OPTIONAL
  EXPORTING
    VALUE(E_XHANDLE) TYPE C.



  e_xhandle = 'X'.

  IF i_fcode <> 'YAAI'.

    CLEAR e_xhandle.

    RETURN.

  ENDIF.

ENDFUNCTION.

3. Open transaction BUS9 and choose New Entries to create a new function code. Set the function code to YAAI and enter AI Assistant as the function text.

Keep the Active by Activity, View, and Sequence Category option selected, and enter 4 (Extras) in the Menu field. Select all checkboxes under Save Mode and Transfer Mode.

Next, double-click Active In Each View on the left, choose New Entries, leave the View field empty, and select all checkboxes under Save Mode and Transfer Mode.

Then, double-click Active In Each View/Screen Sequence Category, choose New Entries, leave the View and Screen Sequence Category fields empty, and select all checkboxes under Save Mode and Transfer Mode.

 

 

 

4. Open transaction BUS7, select the FCODE entry, and then double-click Event → Function Modules. Choose New Entries and enter 9000001 in the Item field. Enter the name of the function module you created, Z_F_EVENT_FCODE_YAAI, select X in the Call field, and enter BUP in the Application field.

 

 

After completing these steps, you should see AI Assistant in the Extras → More Extras menu.

 

Implementing the Instantiation of the Chat User Interface

Let's now implement the instantiation of the chat user interface through which users will interact with the AI Assistant.

For now, we will implement only the minimum code required to display the chat. Later, we will provide system instructions and tools to the AI Assistant.

FUNCTION Z_F_EVENT_FCODE_YAAI
  IMPORTING
    VALUE(I_FCODE) LIKE TBZ4-FCODE OPTIONAL
    VALUE(I_CRSFIELD) LIKE BUS000TBFL-TBFLD OPTIONAL
    VALUE(I_CRSLINE) LIKE SY-LILLI OPTIONAL
  EXPORTING
    VALUE(E_XHANDLE) TYPE C.



  e_xhandle = 'X'.

  IF i_fcode <> 'YAAI'.

    CLEAR e_xhandle.

    RETURN.

  ENDIF.

  IF o_chat IS BOUND.

    o_chat->display( ).

    RETURN.

  ENDIF.

  DATA(lo_openai) = NEW ycl_aai_openai( ).

  o_chat = NEW #( io_api = lo_openai
                  i_greeting = 'How can I help you today?' ).

  o_chat->display( ).

ENDFUNCTION.

Now that the instantiation is implemented, clicking the AI Assistant in the Extras → More Extras menu should display the AI Assistant Chat on the right side of the screen, as illustrated in the following screenshot.

 

At this point, the AI Assistant would be able to help users by answering their questions, but it would not have instructions or context beyond what the user might provide.

Implementing the Tools

Interacting with an LLM (Large Language Model) directly within an SAP transaction is useful, but we can achieve much more. By providing tools, we can enable the LLM to interact directly with the system, access contextual information, and perform actions on behalf of the user.

For this example, we will keep the implementation simple by creating tools that allow the AI Assistant to retrieve information about the current context of the BP transaction. Specifically, the context will include the validation messages displayed to the user when they attempt to save changes, as well as some basic information about the Business Partner being edited.

BP Transaction Context

To provide contextual information to the AI Assistant, we need to collect and store it in memory. For this example, we will create a class named ZCL_BP_CONTEXT to store the context using static attributes. This will allow us to retrieve this information later using the tools that we will create.

Create a class named ZCL_BP_CONTEXT with the following code:

CLASS zcl_bp_context DEFINITION
  PUBLIC
  FINAL
  CREATE PUBLIC .

  PUBLIC SECTION.

    CONSTANTS mc_msgid TYPE bapiret2-id VALUE 'ZBP' ##NO_TEXT.

    CLASS-DATA: mt_messages TYPE bapiret2_t READ-ONLY.

    CLASS-DATA: ms_but000  TYPE but000 READ-ONLY,
                ms_address TYPE bapibus1006_address READ-ONLY.

    CLASS-METHODS set_data
      IMPORTING
        i_s_but000  TYPE but000 OPTIONAL
        i_s_address TYPE bapibus1006_address OPTIONAL.

    CLASS-METHODS add_message
      IMPORTING
        i_s_msg TYPE bapiret2.

    CLASS-METHODS add_messages
      IMPORTING
        i_t_msg TYPE bapiret2_t.

    CLASS-METHODS reset.

  PROTECTED SECTION.
  PRIVATE SECTION.
ENDCLASS.



CLASS zcl_bp_context IMPLEMENTATION.

  METHOD set_data.

    IF i_s_but000 IS SUPPLIED.
      ms_but000 = i_s_but000.
    ENDIF.

    IF i_s_address IS SUPPLIED.
      ms_address = i_s_address.
    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD add_message.

    IF i_s_msg-number IS INITIAL.
      RETURN.
    ENDIF.

    DATA(ls_msg) = i_s_msg.

    IF ls_msg-id IS INITIAL.
      ls_msg-id = mc_msgid.
    ENDIF.

    IF ls_msg-type IS INITIAL.
      ls_msg-type = 'E' ##NO_TEXT.
    ENDIF.

    " If it is a SAP standard error message, then we need to discard all other messages
    " because the system doesn't call all BAdIs when standard validations fail, and
    " consequently, we are not able to update the context accordingly.
    IF ls_msg-type = 'E' AND ls_msg-id(1) <> 'Z' .

      FREE mt_messages.

      APPEND ls_msg TO mt_messages.

    ELSE.

      READ TABLE mt_messages TRANSPORTING NO FIELDS
        WITH KEY
          id = ls_msg-id
          type = ls_msg-type
          number = ls_msg-number
          message_v1 = ls_msg-message_v1
          message_v2 = ls_msg-message_v2
          message_v3 = ls_msg-message_v3
          message_v4 = ls_msg-message_v4.

      IF sy-subrc <> 0.
        APPEND ls_msg TO mt_messages.
      ENDIF.

    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD add_messages.

    " Discard messages from previous check
    IF i_t_msg IS NOT INITIAL AND i_t_msg[ 1 ]-parameter IS NOT INITIAL.

      DELETE mt_messages WHERE parameter = i_t_msg[ 1 ]-parameter.

    ENDIF.

    LOOP AT i_t_msg ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_message>).

      add_message( <ls_message> ).

    ENDLOOP.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD reset.

    FREE mt_messages.

    CLEAR: ms_but000,
           ms_address.

  ENDMETHOD.

ENDCLASS.

BP Transaction Context Tools

Now that we have the class that will hold the contextual information in memory, let's implement the tools that will provide it to the AI Assistant.

Create a class named ZCL_BP_CONTEXT_TOOLS with the following code:

CLASS zcl_bp_context_tools DEFINITION
  PUBLIC
  FINAL
  CREATE PUBLIC .

  PUBLIC SECTION.

    METHODS get_bp_basic_info
      RETURNING VALUE(r_response) TYPE string.

    METHODS get_messages
      RETURNING VALUE(r_response) TYPE string.

  PROTECTED SECTION.

  PRIVATE SECTION.

ENDCLASS.



CLASS zcl_bp_context_tools IMPLEMENTATION.

  METHOD get_bp_basic_info.

    r_response = space.

    IF zcl_bp_context=>ms_but000 IS INITIAL.

      r_response = |No information available. Instruct the user to execute the check on the BP transaction|.
      r_response = |{ r_response } using either the Check button or the F8 key.|.

      RETURN.

    ENDIF.

    r_response = |Partner: { zcl_bp_context=>ms_but000-partner ALPHA = OUT }|.
    r_response = |{ r_response }{ cl_abap_char_utilities=>newline }First Name: { zcl_bp_context=>ms_but000-name_first }|.
    r_response = |{ r_response }{ cl_abap_char_utilities=>newline }Last Name: { zcl_bp_context=>ms_but000-name_last }|.

    IF zcl_bp_context=>ms_address IS NOT INITIAL.

      r_response = |{ r_response }{ cl_abap_char_utilities=>newline }BP Address|.

CLASS zcl_im_bupa_addr_check IMPLEMENTATION.

  METHOD if_ex_bupa_addr_check~check.

    CONSTANTS: lc_msgid     TYPE bapiret2-id VALUE 'ZBP',
               lc_parameter TYPE bapiret2-parameter VALUE 'BUPA_ADDR_CHECK'.

    DATA: l_post_code TYPE string,
          l_city      TYPE string,
          l_prefix    TYPE string.


    IF is_address IS NOT INITIAL.

      " Add BP info to the context
      zcl_bp_context=>set_data(
        EXPORTING
          i_s_address = is_address
      ).

    ENDIF.

    IF is_address-postl_cod1 IS NOT INITIAL AND is_address-country = 'PT'.

      l_post_code = |{ is_address-postl_cod1 }|.
      l_city = to_upper( condense( is_address-city ) ).

      " 1. Validate the postal code format
      IF l_post_code IS INITIAL OR
         strlen( l_post_code ) <> 8 OR
         l_post_code+4(1) <> '-'.

        " The postal code must have the format NNNN-NNN
        APPEND VALUE #( id = lc_msgid
                        number = '001'
                        type = 'E'
                        parameter = lc_parameter ) TO et_return.

      ELSE.

        " Check that the remaining characters are numeric
        DATA(l_digits) = l_post_code(4) && l_post_code+5(3).

        IF NOT l_digits CO '0123456789' OR strlen( condense( l_digits ) ) <> 7.

          " The postal code must contain seven digits
          APPEND VALUE #( id = lc_msgid
                          number = '002'
                          type = 'E'
                          parameter = lc_parameter ) TO et_return.

        ELSE.

          " 2. Extract the first four digits
          l_prefix = l_post_code(4).

          CASE l_city.

            WHEN 'LISBON' OR 'LISBOA'.

              IF l_prefix(1) <> '1'.

                " The postal code prefix is inconsistent with Lisbon
                APPEND VALUE #( id = lc_msgid
                                number = '003'
                                type = 'E'
                                message_v1 = is_address-city
                                parameter = lc_parameter ) TO et_return.

              ENDIF.

            WHEN 'PORTO'.

              IF l_prefix(1) <> '4'.

                " The postal code prefix is inconsistent with Porto
                APPEND VALUE #( id = lc_msgid
                                number = '003'
                                type = 'E'
                                message_v1 = is_address-city
                                parameter = lc_parameter ) TO et_return.

              ENDIF.

            WHEN OTHERS.
              " No city/prefix rule defined for this city

          ENDCASE.

        ENDIF.

      ENDIF.

    ENDIF.

    IF is_address IS NOT INITIAL AND et_return[] IS INITIAL.

      " Personal address data of business partner is error-free.
      APPEND VALUE #( id = lc_msgid
                      number = '004'
                      type = 'S'
                      parameter = lc_parameter ) TO et_return.

    ENDIF.

    " Add messages to the context
    zcl_bp_context=>add_messages( et_return ).

  ENDMETHOD.

ENDCLASS.

CLASS zcl_bupa_person_address_tools IMPLEMENTATION.

  METHOD read_bupa_address_from_memory.

    FREE r_response.

    me->_get_bupa_address_from_memory(
      IMPORTING
        e_s_address_value = DATA(ls_address_personal_value)
    ).

    DATA(ls_bupa_address) = VALUE zst_bupa_address_tool( street      = ls_address_personal_value-street

                                                         house_num2  = ls_address_personal_value-house_num2

                                                         post_code   = ls_address_personal_value-post_code1
                                                         country     = ls_address_personal_value-country ).

      r_response = /ui2/cl_json=>serialize( data = ls_bupa_address ).
    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD read_bupa_address_from_screen.

    FREE r_response.

    ASSIGN ('(SAPLSZA7)ADDR2_DATA') TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<addr2_data>).

    IF <addr2_data> IS NOT ASSIGNED OR <addr2_data> IS INITIAL.
      r_response = 'Business Partner address is not available.'.
      RETURN.
    ENDIF.

    DATA(ls_addr2_data_subset) = CORRESPONDING ty_addr2_data_subset_s( <addr2_data> ).

    DATA(ls_bupa_address) = VALUE zst_bupa_address_tool( street     = ls_addr2_data_subset-street
                                                         house_num1 = ls_addr2_data_subset-house_num1
                                                         house_num2 = ls_addr2_data_subset-house_num2
                                                         city       = ls_addr2_data_subset-city1
                                                         post_code  = ls_addr2_data_subset-post_code1
                                                         country    = ls_addr2_data_subset-country ).

    IF ls_bupa_address IS NOT INITIAL.
      r_response = /ui2/cl_json=>serialize( data = ls_bupa_address ).
    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD update_bupa_address_on_screen.

    FREE r_response.

    ASSIGN ('(SAPLSZA7)ADDR2_DATA') TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<addr2_data>).

    IF <addr2_data> IS ASSIGNED.

      DATA(lo_aai_util) = NEW ycl_aai_util( ).

      DATA(ls_addr2_subset) = VALUE ty_addr2_data_subset_s( street = lo_aai_util->replace_unicode_escape_seq( CONV #( i_street ) )
                                                            house_num1 = lo_aai_util->replace_unicode_escape_seq( CONV #( i_house_num1 ) )
                                                            house_num2 = lo_aai_util->replace_unicode_escape_seq( CONV #( i_house_num2 ) )
                                                            city1 = lo_aai_util->replace_unicode_escape_seq( CONV #( i_city ) )
                                                            post_code1 = i_post_code
                                                            country = i_country ).

      <addr2_data> = CORRESPONDING #( ls_addr2_subset ).

    ELSE.
      r_response = 'Error while updating the Business Partner address on screen.'.
    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD update_bupa_address_in_memory.

    DATA ls_address_personal_data TYPE addr2_data.

    FREE r_response.

    me->_get_bupa_address_from_memory(
      IMPORTING
        e_s_address_value = DATA(ls_address_personal_value)
        e_s_address_selection = DATA(ls_address_personal_selection)
    ).

    IF ls_address_personal_value IS INITIAL.
      r_response = 'Business Partner address is not available in memory.'.
      RETURN.
    ENDIF.

    ls_address_personal_data = CORRESPONDING #( ls_address_personal_value ).

    DATA(lo_aai_util) = NEW ycl_aai_util( ).

    ls_address_personal_data-street = lo_aai_util->replace_unicode_escape_seq( CONV #( i_street ) ).
    ls_address_personal_data-house_num1 = lo_aai_util->replace_unicode_escape_seq( CONV #( i_house_num1 ) ).
    ls_address_personal_data-house_num2 = lo_aai_util->replace_unicode_escape_seq( CONV #( i_house_num2 ) ).
    ls_address_personal_data-city1 = lo_aai_util->replace_unicode_escape_seq( CONV #( i_city ) ).
    ls_address_personal_data-post_code1 = i_post_code.
    ls_address_personal_data-country = i_country.

    CALL FUNCTION 'ADDR_PERSONAL_UPDATE'
      EXPORTING
        address_handle             = ls_address_personal_selection-addrhandle
        address_number             = ls_address_personal_selection-addrnumber
        address_personal_data      = ls_address_personal_data
        language                   = sy-langu
        nation                     = ls_address_personal_selection-nation
        person_handle              = ls_address_personal_selection-pershandle
        person_number              = ls_address_personal_selection-persnumber
        check_address              = space
      EXCEPTIONS
        parameter_error            = 1
        personal_address_not_exist = 2
        version_not_exist          = 3
        internal_error             = 4
        OTHERS                     = 99.

    IF sy-subrc = 0.
      r_response = 'Business Partner address was updated.'.
    ELSE.
      r_response = 'Business Partner address update failed.'.
    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD _get_bupa_address_from_memory.

    DATA l_field TYPE string.

    DATA: ls_address_personal_selection TYPE addr2_sel,
          ls_address_personal_value     TYPE addr2_val.

    CLEAR: e_s_address_value,
           e_s_address_selection.

    l_field = '(SAPLSZA7)G_PERSON_NUMBER'.
    ASSIGN (l_field) TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<g_person_number>).

    l_field = '(SAPLSZA7)G_ADDRESS_NUMBER'.
    ASSIGN (l_field) TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<g_address_number>).

    l_field = '(SAPLSZA7)G_PERSON_HANDLE'.
    ASSIGN (l_field) TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<g_person_handle>).

    l_field = '(SAPLSZA7)G_ADDRESS_HANDLE'.
    ASSIGN (l_field) TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<g_address_handle>).

    l_field = '(SAPLSZA7)G_NATION'.
    ASSIGN (l_field) TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<g_nation>).

    l_field = '(SAPLSZA7)G_DATE_FROM'.
    ASSIGN (l_field) TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<g_date_from>).

    IF <g_person_number> IS ASSIGNED.
      ls_address_personal_selection-persnumber = <g_person_number>.
    ENDIF.

    IF <g_address_number> IS ASSIGNED.
      ls_address_personal_selection-addrnumber = <g_address_number>.
    ENDIF.

    IF <g_person_handle> IS ASSIGNED.
      ls_address_personal_selection-pershandle = <g_person_handle>.
    ENDIF.

    IF <g_address_handle> IS ASSIGNED.
      ls_address_personal_selection-addrhandle = <g_address_handle>.
    ENDIF.

    IF <g_nation> IS ASSIGNED.
      ls_address_personal_selection-nation = <g_nation>.
    ENDIF.

    IF <g_date_from> IS ASSIGNED.
      ls_address_personal_selection-date = <g_date_from>.
    ENDIF.

    IF ls_address_personal_selection IS INITIAL.
      RETURN.
    ENDIF.

    CALL FUNCTION 'ADDR_PERSONAL_GET'

        iv_current_comm_data       = abap_true
      IMPORTING
        address_personal_value     = ls_address_personal_value
      EXCEPTIONS
        parameter_error            = 1
        address_not_exist          = 2
        person_not_exist           = 3
        version_not_exist          = 4
        internal_error             = 5
        OTHERS                     = 6.

    e_s_address_value = ls_address_personal_value.
    e_s_address_selection = ls_address_personal_selection.
