      ENDIF.

      e_t_files = VALUE #( ( content = cl_http_utility=>encode_x_base64( unencoded = l_image )
                             filename = |screenshot{ l_file_extension }|
                             file_size = xstrlen( l_image )
                             file_type = l_mime_type ) ).

    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD get_clipboard_data.

    DATA lt_data TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_row.

    cl_gui_frontend_services=>clipboard_import(
      IMPORTING
        data                 = lt_data
        length               = DATA(l_length)
      EXCEPTIONS
        cntl_error           = 1                " Control error
        error_no_gui         = 2                " No GUI available
        not_supported_by_gui = 3                " GUI does not support this
        OTHERS               = 4
    ).

    IF sy-subrc <> 0.

      r_response = 'Error while importing data from the clipboard.'.

    ELSE.

      IF lt_data IS INITIAL.
        r_response = 'The clipboard is empty.'.
      ENDIF.

      LOOP AT lt_data ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<l_row>).

        IF r_response IS INITIAL.
          r_response = <l_row>.
        ELSE.
          r_response = |{ r_response }{ cl_abap_char_utilities=>newline }{ <l_row> }|.
        ENDIF.

      ENDLOOP.

    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD set_clipboard_data.

    DATA lt_data TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_row.

    DATA l_rc TYPE i.

    SPLIT i_clipboard_data AT cl_abap_char_utilities=>newline INTO TABLE lt_data.

    cl_gui_frontend_services=>clipboard_export(
      IMPORTING
        data                 = lt_data                 " Data
      CHANGING
        rc                   = l_rc                 " Return Code
      EXCEPTIONS
        cntl_error           = 1                " Control error
        error_no_gui         = 2                " No GUI available
        not_supported_by_gui = 3                " GUI does not support this
        no_authority         = 4                " Authorization check failed
        OTHERS               = 5
    ).

    IF sy-subrc <> 0 OR l_rc <> 0.

      r_response = 'Error while exporting data to the clipboard.'.

    ELSE.

      LOOP AT lt_data ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<l_row>).

        IF r_response IS INITIAL.
          r_response = <l_row>.
        ELSE.
          r_response = |{ r_response }{ cl_abap_char_utilities=>newline }{ <l_row> }|.
        ENDIF.

      ENDLOOP.

    ENDIF.

  ENDMETHOD.

ENDCLASS.

In case you want to test these tools, edit the function module Z_F_EVENT_FCODE_YAAI and update its code by adding them in the lo_function_calling->add_methods method call, similarly to what we did when we added the Personal Address tools.

Other examples of tools you can build:

  • Call a transaction, similar to a drill-down report.
  • Perform background tasks.
  • Read, write, upload, and download files.
  • Send emails.
  • ... and certainly many, many more! 🙂

A System-Wide Entry Point: Adding the AI Assistant to MENUSYST

As discussed in the General Technical Prerequisites section, adding an entry point for the AI Assistant usually means finding a suitable enhancement for each transaction. There is another option: adding an item to the SAP standard system menu, MENUSYST, to provide a common way to launch the Assistant across transactions, without enhancing each transaction’s user interface individually.

I'm generally opposed to modifying SAP standard objects. I would consider it only in very exceptional cases and only when the change poses no risk to the system’s existing functionality. This approach does involve a standard-system change, which may require minor adjustments during upgrades.

The required changes are:

Transaction: SE41

Program: MENUSYST

Status: MEN

 

 

Transaction: SE37

Function Module: HELP_START

 

With this approach, we can provide a system-wide entry point that determines whether the AI Assistant can be launched in the current transaction and, if so, which assistant to instantiate, along with the appropriate system instructions and tools.

 

 

Closing Thoughts

That's it for this post! I hope the ideas and examples shared here give you a good starting point for integrating AI assistants into your SAP system.

There are many ways to approach this, and the right solution will depend on the transactions you want to enhance and the extension options available in your SAP environment.

I'd love to hear about your experiences, what you build, and what you learn along the way.

entry.title: SAP TechEd 2026 Berlin: Key Innovations, AI Breakthroughs and What's New in the SAP Ecosystem
entry.content:
SAP TechEd 2026 brings a new wave of enterprise innovation, putting AI agents, Joule Work, intelligent automation and connected business data at the center of the Autonomous Enterprise vision.

SAP TechEd 2026, held in Berlin, highlights SAP's continued commitment to transforming how businesses operate through artificial intelligence, intelligent automation and next-generation enterprise solutions.

This year's announcements reflect a major shift in SAP's AI strategy: moving beyond AI-powered assistance toward autonomous enterprise operations, where AI agents can understand business objectives, coordinate workflows, interact with enterprise applications and execute complex tasks with appropriate governance.

From enhancements to Joule Work and Joule Studio to the introduction of SAP Business AI Platform capabilities, SAP Business Data Cloud innovations and new AI models, TechEd 2026 introduces several developments that will shape the future of enterprise technology.

Let's explore the key announcements and innovations from SAP TechEd 2026.

1. Joule Work: Moving Towards Autonomous Business Operations

One of the biggest highlights of SAP TechEd 2026 is the continued evolution of Joule Work, SAP's AI-powered user experience designed to simplify complex business operations.

Joule Work enables users to describe a business goal in natural language, while AI orchestrates the required agents, applications and data across SAP and non-SAP systems to accomplish the task.

Some of the key enhancements include:

  • Advanced agentic thinking: Improved reasoning, planning and execution capabilities for complex business workflows.
  • Enterprise governance: Built-in audit trails, role-based permissions and human-in-the-loop checkpoints.
  • Expanded SAP Knowledge Graph integration: Better business context to help AI agents understand customer-specific processes and data.
  • Secure agent-to-agent interoperability: Improved connectivity between SAP Joule Agents and third-party AI agents through a secure gateway.

These developments represent an important step toward an enterprise environment where AI agents can collaborate and execute connected business processes securely.

2. Joule Studio: Simplifying Enterprise AI Agent Development

SAP is also expanding Joule Studio, making it easier for developers and business users to build, customize and manage AI agents.

With deeper integration into Joule Work, Joule Studio provides a shared environment for creating custom agents, extending existing Joule Agents and orchestrating workflows.

Key innovations include:

  • Intent-based development: Developers can describe business requirements, and Joule Studio helps identify relevant processes, APIs, data and authorizations.
  • AI agent extensions: Existing Joule Agents can be enhanced with additional instructions, APIs, MCP connections and workflow triggers.
  • n8n integration: Enables orchestration of complex workflows across SAP and non-SAP applications.
  • Agent lifecycle management: New capabilities for testing, evaluating, deploying and monitoring agents.
  • Developer flexibility: Business users can define requirements through the web experience, while developers can continue working through their preferred IDE and CLI tools.

SAP is also introducing pre-deployment testing and offline evaluations to help organizations validate agent behavior before production deployment.

The objective is to make enterprise AI development more accessible while maintaining the governance and security required for business-critical applications.

3. SAP Business AI Platform: Building the Foundation for Enterprise AI

The SAP Business AI Platform is a major part of SAP's Autonomous Enterprise strategy.

It brings together the capabilities required to build, contextualize, reason and govern enterprise AI solutions.

The platform focuses on combining business process knowledge, trusted enterprise data, AI models and governance capabilities to help organizations move beyond isolated AI pilots.

Key announcements include:

SAP Enterprise AI Gateway

A new centralized governance solution designed to manage AI interactions across enterprise environments.

It will provide:

  • Centralized authentication and authorization.
  • AI traffic routing and policy enforcement.
  • Monitoring and usage tracking.
  • Auditing and governance.
  • Secure connectivity across MCPs, APIs, AI agents and large language models.

Built on SAP Integration Suite, the solution aims to simplify the management of enterprise AI interactions.

General availability is planned for Q1 2027.

SAP AI Agent Hub

SAP is expanding AI agent governance capabilities to provide better visibility and control over SAP and third-party AI agents.

A new AI Governance Assistant will also help organizations assess AI systems against regulatory requirements, including the EU AI Act.

This will support risk classification, documentation reviews and ongoing compliance assessments.

4. SAP Business Data Cloud: Advancing Enterprise Data Management

Data remains one of the most important foundations for successful enterprise AI adoption.

At TechEd 2026, SAP announced new SAP Business Data Cloud capabilities designed to make enterprise data more accessible, reusable and valuable for AI and analytics.

Some major innovations include:

Expanded Lakehouse Capabilities

SAP is introducing native support for Apache Iceberg and a distributed SQL query engine, supported by Dremio technology.

These capabilities will help organizations access and process SAP and third-party data across hybrid and multi-cloud environments.

Potential benefits include:

  • Reduced data duplication.
  • Faster access to business insights.
  • Improved query performance.
  • Greater flexibility in data architecture.
  • Consistent governance across data environments.

SAP Business Data Cloud Ontology Manager

A new AI-assisted solution designed to help organizations create and manage domain-specific business ontologies.

It will enable businesses to organize relationships, rules and processes into reusable business context that AI agents can understand.

Enhanced SAP Knowledge Graph

SAP Knowledge Graph will gain support for additional SAP-managed and customer-managed data products.

This will help Joule and other AI agents understand company-specific business relationships and provide more relevant, context-aware responses.

Together, these innovations strengthen SAP's business data fabric strategy and provide a more reliable foundation for enterprise AI.

5. SAP HANA Cloud: AI-Powered Database Administration

SAP is bringing new agentic AI capabilities to SAP HANA Cloud to simplify database administration.

Database administrators will be able to use a conversational interface to perform tasks such as:

  • Monitoring database health.
  • Troubleshooting technical issues.
  • Optimizing SQL queries and database performance.
  • Managing database lifecycle operations.
  • Diagnosing and resolving operational issues.

These capabilities aim to reduce repetitive administrative work and allow database teams to focus on strategic activities.

General availability is planned for Q4 2026.

6. SAP-RPT AI Models: Smarter Predictions and Business Decisions

SAP is expanding its SAP-RPT family of AI models to improve the way AI understands and works with structured enterprise data.

Unlike traditional large language models, which primarily focus on unstructured information, tabular AI is designed to understand structured business data and support more accurate predictions.

Three important developments were announced:

  • SAP-RPT-TS: A time-series forecasting model designed for business scenarios such as demand forecasting. Generally available.
  • SAP-RPT-Decisions: A decision intelligence model designed to automate business decisions across workflows. General availability planned for Q4 2026.
  • SAP-RPT-2: An expanded model supporting multi-table processing, anomaly detection and structured data embeddings. General availability planned for Q1 2027.

SAP also announced the deployment of SAP-RPT on HPE Spaceborne Computer-2 aboard the International Space Station, demonstrating the potential of enterprise AI in edge-computing environments.

7. SAP Document AI: Advancing Intelligent Document Processing

SAP is introducing new capabilities in SAP Document AI to make document processing more intelligent and autonomous.

The new SAP-DOC-1 AI model is designed to extract information from different document formats without extensive upfront configuration.

Additional enhancements include:

  • Document splitting for processing complex, multi-page documents.
  • Custom prompting to define specific information extraction requirements.
  • Deeper integration with Joule Work.
  • Joule Studio capabilities for building document-aware agents and workflows.

These developments will help businesses automate document-intensive processes and reduce manual intervention.

General availability is planned for Q1 2027.

8. SAP Integration Suite: Stronger Connectivity and AI-Driven Integration

As enterprises adopt more AI agents, seamless connectivity between applications and systems becomes increasingly important.

SAP Integration Suite is receiving several enhancements to support modern integration requirements.

Key announcements include:

  • AI-assisted message processing error resolution.
  • AI-based detection of unusual API request payload sizes.
  • Enhanced GitHub integration for managing integration artifacts.
  • Native RosettaNet support for B2B and supply chain integration.
  • New third-party application adapters for Gmail, Google Sheets, GoToWebinar, Microsoft Excel and Salesforce Service Cloud.
  • Improved monitoring through SAP Cloud ALM.

These enhancements will help organizations simplify integration development, improve operational visibility and prepare their enterprise landscapes for agentic AI.

9. SAP Cloud ERP and RISE with SAP: AI-Driven Transformation

SAP is also evolving the RISE with SAP methodology to help customers adopt AI more effectively as part of their business transformation journeys.

The upcoming enhancements include:

  • AI-enriched implementation guidance and best practices.
  • Personalized onboarding across SAP Autonomous Suite.
  • AI readiness assessments that connect business priorities with relevant AI use cases.
  • Structured transformation road maps to help organizations measure business value.

The focus is on helping customers move beyond technology implementation and achieve measurable business outcomes through AI adoption.

General availability is planned for Q1 2027.

10. New SAP Certifications and Learning Opportunities

Alongside its technology announcements, SAP is investing in building the skills required for the next generation of enterprise AI professionals.

Two important learning developments include:

SAP Business AI Platform Solution Architect Certification

A new certification designed for developers, consultants, partners and solution architects.

It validates expertise across three major platform pillars:

  • Build.
  • Contextualize and reason.
  • Govern.

Joule Studio Developer Certification

SAP has also introduced a Joule Studio developer certification focused on building, extending and managing enterprise AI agents.

As part of its introductory offer, the certification is available free of charge through December 31, 2026.

These learning opportunities provide SAP professionals with a chance to strengthen their expertise in enterprise AI and agentic development.

What Does SAP TechEd 2026 Mean for the Future of Enterprise Technology?

The announcements at SAP TechEd 2026 highlight a significant evolution in the enterprise software landscape.

SAP is moving toward an ecosystem where AI is not simply an assistant that answers questions but an intelligent capability that understands business context, collaborates with other agents and helps execute business processes.

A few major trends stand out:

  1. From generative AI to agentic AI: AI agents are becoming more capable of planning and executing complex workflows.
  2. From disconnected systems to connected intelligence: SAP is strengthening interoperability across SAP and third-party applications.
  3. From generic AI to business-aware AI: SAP Knowledge Graph and Business Data Cloud provide the context needed for enterprise-specific intelligence.
  4. From AI experimentation to enterprise governance: Security, compliance, monitoring and controlled execution are becoming essential components of AI adoption.
  5. From manual development to intent-based development: Tools such as Joule Studio are making it easier to translate business requirements into AI-powered solutions.

Final Thoughts

SAP TechEd 2026 reinforces SAP's vision of the Autonomous Enterprise, where people, business applications, trusted data and intelligent AI agents work together to simplify operations and accelerate business outcomes.

With innovations across Joule Work, Joule Studio, SAP Business AI Platform, SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP HANA Cloud and SAP Integration Suite, SAP is building the foundation for the next generation of intelligent enterprise solutions.

For SAP customers, developers, consultants and technology professionals, these announcements create exciting opportunities to explore agentic AI, modern enterprise architecture and intelligent automation.

The future of SAP is moving beyond simply running business processes. It is about making those processes more intelligent, connected and autonomous.

SAP TechEd 2026 Innovation News Guide

entry.title: Building and Deploying AI-Powered Applications on SAP BTP Using Claude Code
entry.content:
Building and Deploying AI-Powered Applications on SAP BTP Using Claude Code

A Practical Exploration of SAP AI Core, BTP Destinations, Prompt Engineering and Cloud Foundry Deployment

Introduction

Generative AI is changing how developers approach application development. From building intelligent assistants to integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into enterprise applications, the possibilities are expanding rapidly.

Within the SAP ecosystem, SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP) provides capabilities to build, integrate and deploy enterprise-grade AI-powered applications.

Recently, I explored how Claude Code can be used as part of an AI application development workflow on SAP BTP. During this exploration, I documented the configuration steps, important concepts and deployment process in a practical technical reference.

In this blog, I'd like to share some of the key concepts and learnings from that journey.

 

 

1. Understanding SAP AI Core

SAP AI Core provides a managed environment for integrating AI capabilities into enterprise applications.

It allows applications to interact with supported Large Language Models and provides an enterprise-oriented approach to authentication and connectivity.

Some important concepts include:

  • LLM inference

  • Embeddings

  • Model deployment

  • AI orchestration

The key takeaway is understanding how an application communicates with an AI model through SAP AI Core rather than embedding credentials directly into application code.

2. Understanding the SAP BTP Destination Service

One of the important aspects of enterprise application development is secure connectivity.

SAP BTP Destinations provide centrally managed connection configurations that applications can reference instead of hardcoding connection details.

During my exploration, I focused on:

  • Creating an AI Core service instance.

  • Generating and understanding service keys.

  • Configuring OAuth2 Client Credentials.

  • Mapping service key fields to destination properties.

  • Understanding the difference between application identity and user identity.

A good understanding of destinations makes application connectivity easier to manage and maintain.

3. Prompt Engineering: Defining How Your AI Application Behaves

A model's response depends not only on the model itself but also on how instructions and context are defined.

System prompts help establish the application's role, responsibilities, boundaries and response behavior.

For example, an SAP Procurement Assistant can be instructed to:

  • Retrieve information using available tools.

  • Avoid inventing purchase order or vendor information.

  • Clearly communicate when information is unavailable.

  • Follow defined business and security rules.

The objective is to make AI applications more predictable, consistent and aligned with enterprise requirements.

 

4. From Development to Deployment Using Cloud Foundry

Building an application is only one part of the journey. Making it available in a BTP environment requires proper deployment configuration.

I explored the following concepts:

  • Cloud Foundry API endpoint configuration.

  • SSO-based CLI login.

  • Organization and Space selection.

  • manifest.yml configuration.

  • Service bindings and environment variables.

  • Application deployment using cf push.

Understanding these components helps connect application development with the deployment lifecycle.

5. Exploring MCP and Joule Integration

Another interesting area is connecting AI applications with external tools and enterprise workflows.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized approach for exposing tools and context to compatible AI clients.

My exploration also included the concept of connecting a deployed application with Joule Work Desktop through its connector configuration.

This opens up interesting possibilities for connecting AI assistants with enterprise capabilities.

6. Key Learnings

A few important takeaways from this exercise:

  1. Secure credential management should be considered from the beginning.

  2. BTP Destinations help separate connectivity configuration from application code.

  3. Well-defined system prompts are essential for predictable AI behavior.

  4. Deployment configuration is as important as application development.

  5. AI integration becomes more useful when combined with enterprise context and tools.

Conclusion

This exploration helped me connect several important concepts across SAP BTP, AI Core, prompt engineering and application deployment.

I have also prepared a practical technical reference covering the configuration steps, examples and deployment checklist to make these concepts easier to revisit.

I hope these learnings are useful to SAP developers, architects and technology enthusiasts who are exploring AI-powered application development.

What are your experiences with Claude Code, SAP AI Core and MCP-based integrations? I'd love to hear your thoughts!

Disclaimer: This article reflects my technical exploration and learning. Configuration options and service availability may vary depending on your SAP BTP landscape and entitlements.

entry.title: Beyond Data Silos: Powering the Autonomous Enterprise with SAP's Next-Generation Data Fabric and AI
entry.content:
The next era of enterprise transformation is not just about making data available. It is about making data intelligent, contextual, trusted, and actionable.

Artificial Intelligence is rapidly transforming how businesses operate. From demand forecasting and supply chain optimization to financial planning and customer engagement, AI agents are moving beyond generating insights to actively supporting business decisions and executing complex workflows.

But there is one fundamental challenge: AI is only as intelligent as the business context it understands.

Enterprise data is often scattered across applications, databases, data warehouses, and cloud platforms. Even when organizations have access to vast amounts of information, disconnected systems, inconsistent master data, and fragmented business definitions make it difficult for AI to understand how the business actually operates.

At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP introduced a new wave of innovations in SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) to address this challenge and accelerate the journey toward the autonomous enterprise.

With advancements in open lakehouse architecture, zero-copy data sharing, enterprise master data management, and business knowledge modeling, SAP is taking an important step toward creating an intelligent data foundation where AI agents can understand business operations, make informed decisions, and act with greater autonomy and confidence.

Let's explore the innovations shaping this transformation.

1. Breaking Data Silos: An Open Lakehouse Built for the AI Era

Enterprise data should not be restricted by platforms, storage locations, or technology boundaries. However, traditional data architectures often require organizations to replicate information across multiple systems, creating additional costs, operational complexity, and inconsistent data.

SAP is addressing this challenge by strengthening its open lakehouse foundation through the completed acquisition of Dremio.

The vision is simple: make enterprise data accessible wherever it resides, without constantly moving or duplicating it.

Key innovations include:

  • Open lakehouse architecture: Native Apache Iceberg support and a universal catalog powered by Apache Polaris provide an open foundation for discovering, governing, and sharing enterprise data.

  • Zero-copy data sharing: SAP BDC Connect enables interoperability with platforms such as Databricks, Snowflake, Google Cloud, AWS, and Microsoft, minimizing unnecessary data duplication.

  • Federated data access: Powered by Dremio's high-performance SQL query engine, organizations can query distributed data across SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, and PostgreSQL without physically moving it.

  • Autonomous query optimization: Dremio Reflections intelligently optimize query performance by learning workload patterns and automatically precomputing frequently accessed results.

An especially exciting development is the integration with Joule Work, allowing business users to ask complex questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in trusted enterprise data.

The business impact: Less time managing data pipelines, fewer data silos, faster analytics, and a scalable data foundation for AI agents operating across enterprise environments.

2. SAP and Databricks: Accelerating the Next Generation of Data and AI Innovation

 

The future of enterprise AI requires collaboration between business applications, data engineering platforms, and advanced AI technologies.

SAP's expanded partnership with Databricks brings additional industry-leading capabilities into SAP Databricks within SAP Business Data Cloud.

The expanded capabilities include:

  • Lakeflow

  • Agent Bricks

  • Unity Gateway

  • Lakebase

Through SAP Application Data Foundation, organizations can access SAP application data directly within their preferred SAP BDC engine, including SAP Databricks.

This creates an opportunity to combine the rich business semantics of SAP data with the advanced analytics and AI capabilities of Databricks.

Consider a real-world manufacturing scenario.

A manufacturer wants to predict future product demand, optimize inventory, and improve supply chain efficiency.

Traditionally, this could involve extracting historical sales data, integrating inventory information, combining external market intelligence, and building complex data pipelines before developing forecasting models.

With SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP Databricks, data professionals can access SAP data, enrich it with third-party information, and create custom data products on a semantically rich foundation.

AI models can then generate forecasts that are aligned with the business logic and relationships already embedded in SAP systems.

The business impact: Accelerated AI development, reduced integration complexity, lower total cost of ownership, and faster realization of business value from cloud transformation.

3. SAP Reltio: Turning Fragmented Master Data into a Trusted 360-Degree Business View

 

One of the biggest barriers to enterprise AI adoption is inconsistent master data.

Imagine an organization where the same customer exists in multiple systems with different customer IDs, addresses, names, and transaction histories.

A human employee might recognize that these records represent the same customer. But an AI agent needs reliable entity resolution and connected business relationships to reach the same conclusion.

This is where SAP Reltio becomes important.

Following the completion of its acquisition, SAP Reltio is now generally available within SAP Business Data Cloud, bringing multi-domain Master Data Management (MDM) capabilities natively into the business data fabric.

Its AI-based entity resolution capabilities help organizations:

  • Identify and reconcile duplicate records across SAP and non-SAP systems.

  • Harmonize inconsistent customer, supplier, and product information.

  • Build unified 360-degree views of critical business entities.

  • Connect business attributes, relationships, and interactions.

  • Publish trusted entity profiles as governed data products.

The significance goes beyond traditional master data management.

When Joule and Joule Agents access unified business entity profiles, they gain a more complete understanding of customers, suppliers, products, and their relationships across the enterprise.

For example, a customer service agent can potentially understand a customer's purchase history, outstanding invoices, service interactions, and business relationships through connected and trusted information.

The business impact: Better data quality, improved decision-making, stronger customer intelligence, and a reliable foundation for context-aware enterprise AI.

4. SAP Knowledge Graph and Ontology Manager: Giving AI Agents the Context to Think and Act

 

This is arguably one of the most important developments in SAP's journey toward the autonomous enterprise.

AI agents do not simply need access to information. They need to understand what that information represents, how different business entities are connected, and which business rules govern their decisions.

For example, knowing that an invoice is overdue is useful. But understanding the customer associated with that invoice, the agreed payment terms, the credit exposure, and the organization's collections policies is what enables meaningful business action.

SAP Knowledge Graph provides this connected business understanding by linking enterprise entities, relationships, and business rules.

At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP introduced SAP Business Data Cloud Ontology Manager, an AI-assisted experience that enables organizations to create domain-specific views of SAP Knowledge Graph.

Rather than exposing an entire enterprise knowledge model to every AI agent, organizations can create curated views containing only the information relevant to a particular business scenario.

Consider a collections AI agent.

To support collections operations effectively, the agent needs to understand:

  • Customer relationships.

  • Outstanding invoices.

  • Payment terms.

  • Credit risk.

  • Financial transactions.

  • Relevant business rules and policies.

Using Ontology Manager, organizations can create a dedicated collections domain view that connects these entities and relationships.

Joule Agents can then use this context to generate more relevant answers, recommendations, and business actions.

Even more importantly, these domain-specific views inherit business definitions and governance from SAP Knowledge Graph.

This means organizations can reuse the same business semantics across collections, cash flow management, order management, and other business scenarios without repeatedly redefining the underlying concepts.

The business impact: More intelligent AI agents, consistent business semantics, reusable enterprise knowledge, and decisions grounded in how the organization actually operates.

5. The Bigger Picture: SAP Is Moving Beyond Data Management Toward Business Intelligence for Autonomous Operations

The real significance of these announcements is not any individual technology or product integration. It is how these capabilities come together to create a unified foundation for enterprise intelligence.

Consider how the different innovations complement each other:

SAPinnovationRoleintheautonomousenterprise

Dremio Open Lakehouse

Makes distributed enterprise data accessible

Apache Iceberg and Polaris

Enables open data management and discovery

SAP BDC Connect

Supports zero-copy data sharing

SAP Databricks

Accelerates advanced analytics and AI development

SAP Reltio

Establishes trusted, unified business entities

SAP Knowledge Graph

Connects enterprise data with business meaning

Ontology Manager

Creates reusable, domain-specific business context

Joule and Joule Agents

Turn business context into intelligent assistance and action

 

Together, these capabilities establish a powerful foundation for the next generation of enterprise AI.

The transformation can be understood through four interconnected layers:

The foundation of an autonomous enterprise

AI & Autonomous Actions

Joule · Joule Agents · Intelligent business workflows

 

Business Context & Semantics

SAP Knowledge Graph · Ontology Manager · SAP Reltio

 

Data Integration & Interoperability

SAP BDC Connect · Zero-copy sharing · SAP Databricks

 

Open Data Foundation

Dremio · Apache Iceberg · Apache Polaris · Distributed data sources

Conceptual representation of how the announced capabilities work together, not an official SAP reference architecture.

This approach shifts the enterprise data strategy from simply collecting and processing information to creating a connected business intelligence ecosystem.

6. What Enterprises Should Take Away from These Announcements

For business leaders, enterprise architects, data engineers, and AI transformation teams, these innovations highlight several important priorities:

1. Think beyond traditional data integration. Build open architectures that allow data to remain accessible across platforms without unnecessary duplication.

2. Treat business context as a strategic asset. High-quality data alone is not enough. Business definitions, relationships, policies, and semantics must also be available to AI.

3. Invest in trusted master data. AI-driven decisions require consistent customer, supplier, product, and financial information across systems.

4. Make enterprise knowledge reusable. Domain-specific ontologies can help organizations develop AI agents that understand individual business processes without rebuilding business semantics for every use case.

5. Move from AI experimentation to business execution. The ultimate objective is to enable AI agents to support real business workflows with the appropriate governance, context, and controls.

Conclusion: The Future Belongs to Enterprises That Connect Data, Context, and Intelligence

SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 marks an important milestone in SAP's vision for the autonomous enterprise.

With the evolution of SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP is bringing together open lakehouse architecture, cross-platform data interoperability, advanced analytics, unified master data, enterprise knowledge graphs, and AI-powered business agents.

The bigger opportunity is not simply to make enterprise data available to AI. It is to make enterprise data understandable and actionable.

Imagine an enterprise where AI agents can understand customer relationships, recognize supply chain dependencies, interpret financial policies, evaluate business risks, and recommend or execute actions based on trusted organizational knowledge.

That is the direction SAP Business Data Cloud is helping organizations move toward.

The next competitive advantage will not come from having more data or deploying more AI models. It will come from connecting data with business meaning and enabling intelligent systems to turn that understanding into action.

The autonomous enterprise is no longer just a vision of the future. With trusted data, connected business context, and intelligent AI agents, organizations are beginning to build its foundation today.

Original SAP Announcement: Advancing SAP Lakehouse and New Data Fabric Innovations in SAP Business Data Cloud for the Autonomous Enterprise

entry.title: SAP Joule Work at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026: Redefining the Future of Work with Agentic AI
entry.content:
How SAP is transforming enterprise productivity through an AI-native experience, intelligent agents, connected applications, and autonomous business execution.

The way we interact with enterprise software is about to change significantly.

For decades, employees have worked across multiple business applications, switching between screens, searching for information, navigating workflows, and coordinating activities across different departments. Even with automation and digital transformation, completing a business task often requires interaction with multiple systems.

But what if employees could simply describe what they want to accomplish, and AI could understand the objective, identify the required information, coordinate the relevant agents, and help complete the work?

This is the vision behind SAP Joule Work.

At SAP TechEd Berlin 2026, SAP announced significant advancements in Joule Work, demonstrating how enterprise AI is evolving beyond traditional conversational assistants toward intelligent, context-aware, and agent-driven business execution.

The announcement represents an important shift in SAP's user experience strategy: moving from application-centric interactions to an AI-native experience where business users can focus on outcomes rather than navigating individual applications.

Let's explore what is new in SAP Joule Work and why it matters for the future of enterprise productivity.

1. What Is SAP Joule Work?

 

SAP Joule Work is SAP's AI-powered work experience designed to bring business applications, AI assistants, and intelligent agents together through a unified interface.

Instead of interacting with every application independently, employees can use Joule Work as a central starting point for their daily business activities.

Users can express their requirements in natural language, interact with AI assistants, access relevant business information, and work with agents that help coordinate activities across connected enterprise systems.

The key idea is simple:

Don't make employees navigate the business. Let AI help employees get business work done.

SAP is positioning Joule Work as a new way of experiencing enterprise software, bringing intelligence and business execution closer to where employees actually work.

2. A Completely Redesigned AI-Native User Experience

 

One of the major announcements at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 is the redesigned Joule Work experience.

SAP has reimagined the user experience around a unified entry point, making it more intuitive to interact with business applications and AI capabilities.

The new experience brings together:

  • SAP business applications.

  • Microsoft 365.

  • Claude Cowork.

  • Glean.

  • ServiceNow.

  • SAP Joule Assistants and Joule Agents.

This is particularly interesting because enterprise employees rarely work within a single application ecosystem.

For example, a business user might need information from SAP S/4HANA, collaborate through Microsoft 365, retrieve organizational knowledge from Glean, and coordinate activities through ServiceNow.

Joule Work aims to bring these experiences together rather than forcing employees to continuously switch between different applications.

Another important capability is its ability to remember user preferences and context from previous interactions, allowing the experience to adapt to individual working patterns.

The business impact: A more consistent employee experience, reduced application switching, and easier access to business information and AI capabilities.

3. Conversations and Spaces: Two Important Ways of Working with Joule

 
SAP TechEd highlighted two important elements of the Joule Work experience: Conversations and Spaces.

Conversations – Interact with Enterprise AI Naturally

Conversations provide a natural-language interface for interacting with Joule.

Users can ask questions, request information, seek recommendations, and engage with assistants and agents to accomplish business tasks.

For example:

"Show me the latest sales performance, identify the regions that are below target, and summarize the key reasons for the decline."

Rather than manually navigating multiple reports, users can interact with Joule through a conversational experience to explore business information and obtain relevant insights.

The objective is to make enterprise intelligence accessible through natural interactions.

Spaces – Bring Business Information Together

Spaces provide a collaborative experience where information can be brought together into interactive, reusable work environments.

Instead of keeping business information scattered across conversations and applications, users can work with contextual information and interactive applications within a shared space.

For example, a sales team could use a dedicated space to bring together:

  • Sales performance information.

  • Customer account details.

  • Pipeline insights.

  • Business recommendations.

  • Relevant applications and workflows.

This creates a more structured way to collaborate around specific business objectives.

Why this matters: Conversations help employees interact with AI, while Spaces help organize information and work around business outcomes.

4. Agentic Thinking: Moving from Answering Questions to Completing Complex Workflows

 

This is arguably one of the most important advancements announced for Joule Work at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026.

Traditional AI assistants typically respond to individual prompts or perform predefined tasks.

However, enterprise business processes are rarely simple. A single business objective can involve multiple systems, data sources, departments, and decision points.

SAP is introducing new agentic thinking capabilities in Joule Work to help AI agents plan and orchestrate the steps required to complete complex, multistep business workflows.

These capabilities focus on:

  • Understanding the user's business objective.

  • Planning the steps required to achieve it.

  • Identifying relevant assistants and agents.

  • Coordinating activities across business domains.

  • Orchestrating execution across SAP and non-SAP systems.

A practical business example

Imagine a finance manager asking Joule Work:

"Analyze overdue customer invoices, identify high-risk accounts, prioritize collections activities, and prepare recommendations for the finance team."

This is not a simple question.

To support this request, the system needs to consider:

  1. Customer information and account details.

  2. Outstanding invoices and payment history.

  3. Payment terms and credit exposure.

  4. Relevant business rules.

  5. Prioritized collections recommendations.

With agentic thinking, Joule Work can plan and coordinate the activities required to address the request through relevant assistants and agents.

The goal is to move beyond individual AI responses toward coordinated business execution.

This is where enterprise AI becomes particularly powerful: AI is no longer just responding to instructions; it is helping orchestrate the work required to achieve business outcomes.

5. Open Agent Interoperability: Connecting SAP and Third-Party AI Agents

 

Enterprise AI will not operate within a single technology ecosystem.

Organizations are increasingly adopting different AI platforms, third-party agents, and specialized automation solutions.

Recognizing this, SAP is advancing Joule Work through open interoperability protocols, including:

  • Agent2Agent (A2A): Enables communication and collaboration between different AI agents.

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP): Enables AI applications and agents to connect with external tools and contextual information.

One important enhancement announced at TechEd is the ability for third-party agents to securely invoke Joule Agents through a governed agent gateway.

This creates opportunities for agents operating on different platforms to collaborate within enterprise workflows.

Example: Procurement workflow

Imagine an organization using a third-party procurement agent to identify potential supplier risks.

That agent could securely invoke relevant Joule Agents to obtain SAP business information and support supplier-related processes.

The agents can collaborate across their respective environments, subject to configured access permissions and governance.

This is an important development because it moves enterprise AI away from isolated agents toward a more connected ecosystem.

The future of enterprise AI will depend not only on intelligent agents but also on their ability to communicate and collaborate securely.

6. Personalized AI Experience Across Web, Desktop, Mobile, and Voice

Another interesting aspect of the Joule Work announcement is its cross-device experience.

SAP presented Joule Work as a redesigned experience accessible across multiple interaction channels:

  • Web.

  • Desktop.

  • Mobile.

  • Voice.

  • Apple CarPlay.

This reflects an important change in how employees expect to interact with enterprise applications.

Business users should not need to be sitting in front of a desktop computer to access enterprise intelligence.

For example, a manager travelling between business locations could interact with Joule through supported mobile or voice experiences to access information and stay connected with business activities.

SAP also highlighted the ability to create skills that work across desktop and web experiences, helping provide consistency across different interaction surfaces.

The broader vision is to make enterprise AI available wherever employees need it.

7. Business Context: Making Joule Work Understand Your Organization

An AI assistant can generate answers quickly, but enterprise decisions require more than general knowledge.

An organization has its own business processes, policies, customer relationships, financial rules, and operational dependencies.

For Joule Work to provide meaningful assistance, it needs access to the context that defines how the organization operates.

SAP is enhancing SAP Knowledge Graph capabilities to incorporate additional SAP and non-SAP data sources specific to each customer.

Users can query and explore customized enterprise data using natural language, helping ground AI responses in their own business information.

Consider a sales manager asking:

"Which customers have declining sales, outstanding payments, and high business risk?"

Answering this requires more than retrieving sales figures.

The system needs to connect customer profiles, sales history, invoices, payment information, and relevant business relationships.

By improving access to enterprise-specific knowledge, SAP is working toward making Joule Work more context-aware and relevant to individual organizations.

The real differentiator is not just AI intelligence. It is AI intelligence grounded in your business.

8. SAP Joule Work: What Makes This a Significant Change?

The evolution of Joule Work represents a fundamental shift in how employees interact with enterprise technology.

TraditionalenterpriseexperienceSAPJouleWorkvision

Navigate multiple applications

Unified AI-powered entry point

Search manually for information

Natural-language interactions

Work with individual AI assistants

Coordinate multiple agents

Switch between different systems

Connect SAP and third-party applications

Retain user preferences and interaction context

Work with isolated information

Bring information together through Spaces

Execute multistep tasks manually

Use agentic orchestration to support execution

Access enterprise software primarily through desktops

Interact across web, desktop, mobile, and voice

 

This is more than a new interface. It is a change in the relationship between employees, enterprise applications, and AI.

9. The Bigger Vision: From Application-Centric to Intent-Driven Enterprise

The most important takeaway from SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 is the shift toward an AI-native enterprise experience.

Traditionally, employees have been required to understand application navigation, identify the right transaction, retrieve information, and manually coordinate activities.

With Joule Work, SAP is moving toward a model where employees can express their intent and AI helps coordinate the required activities.

The vision can be summarized in five steps:

The Joule Work experience

  1. Express business intent

    The employee describes the desired business outcome using natural language.

  2. Understand and plan

    Joule interprets the request and plans the activities needed.

  3. Coordinate assistants and agents

    Relevant assistants and agents are orchestrated across business domains.

  4. Connect enterprise systems

    SAP and supported third-party applications provide the required information and capabilities.

  5. Support business execution

    The coordinated workflow helps deliver the requested outcome within configured governance and permissions.

This is the direction SAP is taking toward the autonomous enterprise, where AI becomes an integral part of how business work is performed.

Conclusion: The Future of Work Is Not About More Applications. It Is About Better Outcomes.

SAP Joule Work represents an exciting evolution in enterprise AI.

The announcements at SAP TechEd Berlin 2026 demonstrate SAP's ambition to transform the employee experience through a unified AI interface, intelligent agent orchestration, connected applications, personalized interactions, and enterprise-specific business context.

What makes this transformation particularly interesting is the move away from application-centric working toward intent-driven execution.

Employees should be able to focus on what needs to be achieved rather than spending time figuring out where information resides or which application to use.

With Joule Work, SAP is working toward a future where conversations become workflows, agents become collaborators, and enterprise applications become part of a connected AI experience.

The next generation of enterprise productivity will not be measured by how many applications employees use, but by how effectively they achieve business outcomes.

And that is what makes SAP Joule Work an important development in the journey toward the autonomous enterprise.

entry.title: CDS View Extensions in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: Architecture, Tools, and What Matters
entry.content:
***Applies to: SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2023 FPS01 and later. CDS extension mechanics apply from S/4HANA 1909 onwards; the Joule connectivity described here requires 2023 FPS01+***

Part 1 of 2 | Series: Your SAP S/4HANA Data Model Is Your AI Strategy

Picture this scenario. As part of an SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition transformation project, your company has just enabled Joule on the SAP Fiori Launchpad. The demo has gone well. The finance lead is keen. Within the first week she asks: "Can Joule tell me the margin by our internal product tier classification?"

The answer is it cannot. Not because Joule can’t surface it, but because your product tier classification has been sitting in a Z-table since the SAP ERP days and was never added to any CDS view. From where Joule sits, that data does not exist. The same gap is blocking the OData API your integration team wants to expose. The same gap is blocking the SAC model your analytics team is trying to build.

One missing CDS extension. Three blocked workstreams.

That is the argument for getting CDS extensions right. Not one platform. All of them.

Supporting customers in my role as SAP S/4HANA RIG solution architect, I see this pattern on almost every transformation engagement and it rarely arrives alone.

Now picture the procurement lead sends a different request that same week: "Can we get planned delivery time into the purchasing analytics dashboard?"  This one looks identical from the outside - another field Joule and SAC cannot see - but the cause is different. Planned delivery time already exists in SAP’s database. It is standard SAP data that simply has not been promoted to any released CDS view. No Z-table, no custom logic, but the fix is not the same either.

Two situations. Same symptom. Different cause. Different path. Let's work through both.

The SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition Context

In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, SAP manages the HANA database, application server, and OS layers on hyperscaler or SAP’s own infrastructure. You own the application configuration, the transport landscape, and the extension estate. That split matters more than it sounds.

The release rhythm is: a base release every two years (S/4HANA 2023, 2025, 2027), Feature Pack Stacks every six months within a base release, delivering incremental innovations, and Support Pack Stacks after mainstream cutover, carrying only fixes. Mainstream maintenance runs seven years per base release. Under RISE with SAP, SAP executes the upgrade; you own the readiness work and the cutover decision.

In practice, that means upgrade preparation sits on your plate, and the quality of your extension determines how much of that preparation is analysis versus remediation.

Here is what upgrade readiness actually means for extensions. SAP runs the Software Update Manager (SUM) against your development system. As part of that process, ABAP activation checks run against every object in the customer namespace. Any extension that references an internal SAP object that has changed, which can be a view structure, a table field, or an association cardinality, will throw an activation error. Those errors block the transport chain. You cannot promote to QA or production until every activation failure in the development system is resolved, re-tested and re-transported. On a program with 50–100 custom extension objects, even three or four failures, you can add hours to days to a cutover window that is usually already tight.

The mechanism that prevents this is the C1 release contract. When SAP marks a CDS view as C1-released, it is a formal architectural commitment: the view's interface, its field names, types, and association signatures, will not change in ways that break downstream consumers. If your extension targets a C1-released view using EXTEND VIEW ENTITY, SAP owns the upgrade compatibility. If you've extended an unreleased view, used a Z-copy of a standard view, or written Classic ABAP that reads internal table structures directly, there is no contract and no guarantee. The ABAP Test Cockpit (ATC) will tell you how exposed you are; running it against your extension estate before each FPS is not optional, it's the earliest point at which you find out what needs to be fixed.

On-premise teams have exactly the same structural problem. The difference is that on-premise teams control the upgrade schedule and can defer it. In SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, that deferral option is limited; you stay current, or you fall out of mainstream maintenance. That is why the extension quality conversation that on-premise programs have been able to postpone tends to arrive earlier and more urgently for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition.

The Extensibility Stack: Where CDS Extensions Fit

SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition supports the full SAP extensibility portfolio. Understanding where CDS extensions sit within it matters before choosing your approach.

CDS view extensions, written as EXTEND VIEW ENTITY in ADT, sit in the Developer In-App tier. When targeting C1-released views, they are Level A: ABAP Cloud compliant and fully upgrade-safe.

One practical note specific to SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition: in a system configured with the ABAP Cloud language version, the compiler will reject references to unreleased objects. This is not a warning; it is a build failure. That enforcement mechanism is one of the more useful guardrails the platform provides.

Clean Core, Release Contracts, and Upgrade Safety

The A–D Classification

SAP's Clean Core framework maps to something concrete: whether your extension object activates cleanly after an upgrade without manual intervention.

Level

What it means

CDS extensions land here when...

A

ABAP Cloud compliant, released objects only

Targeting C1/C0-released views with EXTEND VIEW ENTITY

B

Stable interfaces, not fully cloud-ready

Extending views with partial release contracts

C

References internal SAP artifacts

Using unreleased views or internal objects

D

Direct modification of SAP standard

Not appropriate


Level A costs upfront discipline — checking release contracts, following the bottom-up propagation pattern, using the right syntax. That investment is front-loaded: a few extra steps at build time that translate into a quieter, lower-risk upgrade cycle. Level C and D extensions tend to surface at upgrade time as activation failures that need to be resolved before cutover.

Release Contracts

Before extending any CDS view, check its release contract. This is the formal binding between SAP and you on interface stability.

Contract

Name

What it means

What it enables

C0

Extend

Stability at defined extension points only. Has two visibility scopes: Use in Key User Apps or Use in Cloud Development — or both

CDS view extensions, append structures, BAdIs. Use in Key User Apps scope makes the view available in Custom Fields & Logic (F1481) and SCFD_REGISTRY tools

C1

Use System-Internally

Stable public interface guaranteed for use within the ABAP system. SAP will not change the interface in ways that break downstream consumers after an upgrade

Using the view as a data source in custom ABAP development within the same system

C2

Use as Remote API

Stable public interface guaranteed for use outside the ABAP system

Consuming the view via OData, remote function calls, or external API clients

No contract / internal

Unreleased

No stability guarantee — SAP can change or remove the object without notice

Nothing. Referencing these places your extension at Level C or D in the clean core classification

In ADT, open the target view and navigate to the API State tab. A C1 or C0 contract means SAP has committed to not changing the interface in ways that break extensions. @vdm.lifecycle.contract.type: #PUBLIC_LOCAL_API is a further contract type indicating a stable, released public interface — also safe to build on.

The Virtual Data Model: Your Extension Target

SAP's Virtual Data Model is a semantic stack with deliberate layering:The rule that matters most: extend at the lowest layer where the data lives and let it propagate up. If you only extend the consumption view, the OData service bound to the interface view won't see your field. If you extend the interface view, every consumer up the stack including OData, SAC, Fiori, Joule inherits it automatically.

You can see this layering live in the Fiori View Browser app (F2170). Search for I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01, which is the view used in the code examples throughout this post. The results list shows its VDM View Type as Basic, confirming this is the interface layer: above the physical database, below the consumption views. This is the layer your extension targets.

In ADT, the view type is declared explicitly on every SAP-delivered VDM view via @vdm.viewType: #BASIC, #COMPOSITE, or #CONSUMPTION. This annotation drives behaviour in SAC, Embedded Analytics, and Fiori Elements, and tells you which layer you're working with before writing a single line of extension code.

Never extend P_* (private) views: no release contract, subject to change by SAP without notice.

Two Kinds of Data Gap

Two distinct situations produce the same symptom - a consumer that cannot find the data it needs. Diagnosing which one you are dealing with determines your path.

Gap 1: A Standard SAP Field Not Yet Exposed

The field exists in a standard SAP table, such as EKPO, MARA, LFA1, VBAP, but no released CDS view has ever selected it. This is more common than expected. SAP has exposed the majority of high-traffic fields through released views, but the long tail of table columns that matter to specific business scenarios is substantial.

First step: confirm with Alternative Search in View Browser (F2170)

Before concluding a field is unavailable, use the Alternative Search function. Open the View Browser (F2170), switch to the Alternative Search tab, and enter the table name and field name. This searches across all released CDS views for any that read that field from that table — including views you would not have found by name.

If no results carry the Released status, even if internal views reference the field, it is not accessible through any stable CDS interface. PLIFZ returns 86 views in this search shown above. None are Released. From Joule, SAC, or any OData client, this field does not exist.

Once confirmed, three paths forward in clean core preference order:

Option 1 — Key User path (cleanest)

Check whether the field's business context is available in the Custom Fields app (F1481). If it is, add the field as a key user extension. SAP handles CDS propagation and OData registration automatically. No developer code required and the result is Level A clean core.

Option 2 — Wrapper view (developer path)

If the key user path is not available, build a minimal custom CDS view that reads the fields directly from the SAP standard table, then extend the released interface view with an association to this wrapper. The wrapper reads unreleased SAP table structures — Level C in the clean core model. It works and can be made stable, but it carries an upgrade risk if SAP restructures the underlying table. Document it explicitly, add the base table to your Simplification List checks before each FPS and track it as technical debt until SAP delivers a clean release.

Note on ABAP Cloud mode: In an SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition system configured with ABAP Cloud language version, direct access to unreleased tables like EKPO will be rejected at compile time. Option 1 or Option 3 are the only supported paths in that configuration.

-- Wrapper view: reads unreleased SAP table directly (Level C in clean core)
-- Only build this after confirming the field is not already exposed
-- using Alternative Search in View Browser (F2170)

Option 3 — Request SAP to release the field

Submit a feature request via . SAP reviews these and adds fields to released CDS views based on demand. The right long-term resolution when the field is strategically important, and the wrapper approach introduces unacceptable upgrade risk.

Gap 2: Custom Business Data

If the data was never part of SAP's standard model — it lives in a Z-table carried over from an SAP ERP landscape, or was built fresh during the current implementation — Alternative Search will return nothing by design. The field isn't missing from SAP's views; it simply doesn't exist in SAP's data model at all.

The resolution here is the developer extension pattern: build a CDS view on your custom table, then extend the relevant SAP interface view with an association to it. The data stays in your Z-table, the CDS layer becomes the bridge. Every consumer above, including OData, SAC, Fiori, Joule, gains access through that association. The worked example later in this post walks through this .

The Extension Toolkit: Key User and Developer Paths

Once you know what gap you are filling, you have two supported extension paths in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. They are deliberately separate and cannot directly consume each other's outputs.

The Key User Lane

Custom Fields app (F1481) — No ABAP, no ADT. Create custom fields, extend data sources, and implement custom logic within a form-based UI. When a view is available as a data source in this app, the platform handles CDS propagation, OData registration, and Fiori field placement automatically. The result is Level A clean core.

Custom CDS Views app (F1866A) — A guided SAP Fiori application for building analytical and external API views without code. Select a scenario (Analytical Cube, Standard CDS View, or External API), choose from released SAP data sources, define joins through a form, and activate. The system generates the CDS source.

Use it when: your requirement is analytical reporting or a simple external API, all data sources are released SAP views, and the logic fits what the form can express.

Hard limits: you cannot use it if you need association-based views also exposed as OData (mutually exclusive in the app) or if your data source is a Z-table. Custom CDS Views created here carry no C1 release contract. In ABAP Cloud development (the standard for Level A clean core), they cannot be consumed as a data source. Classic ABAP can access them, but at the cost of coupling key user and developer extensibility layers, which is worth documenting as a dependency. The reverse also holds: views extended through ADT cannot be used as data sources in the app.

The Developer Lane

Code-first, full CDS DDL language, managed in your own development project in ADT. This is the path for anything the app can't handle: extending existing SAP views bottom-up through the full VDM stack, working with RAP business objects, or building the data model foundation that feeds a Joule skill.

The template you select in the ADT New Data Definition wizard depends on the base view type:

  • define view → select Extend View template → syntax: extend view Base with ExtensionName { }
  • define view entity → select Extend View Entity template → syntax: extend view entity Base with { }

Most standard SAP VDM views in older S/4HANA releases use the classic define view syntax. Newer RAP-based views use define view entity. Always check the first line of the target view in ADT — the two syntaxes are not interchangeable.

Before You Extend: Three Checks

Whether you're coming from Gap 1 or Gap 2, these checks apply to the target view before writing extension code.

  1. API State in ADT: C1, C0, or #PUBLIC_LOCAL_API contract. @Metadata.allowExtensions: true indicates direct metadata extension support. Registration in SCFD_REGISTRY (check 2) is the complementary signal for field-list extensions via EXTEND VIEW ENTITY.

  1. SCFD_REGISTRY: Views registered here are explicitly designed for extension. The Custom Fields app (F1481) can also drive extensions to them.

  1. Structural blockers — Views using GROUP BY, UNION, or UNION ALL cannot have their select list extended. Check @AbapCatalog.viewEnhancementCategory. If it's #NONE, build a custom view on top instead.

The Core Pattern: Extending for Custom Business Data

The following section works through a complete extension for the Gap 2 scenario: custom business data in a Z-table that needs to be visible to Joule, SAC, and a custom OData service.

Choosing your method

Before writing a line of code, understand which of the three developer-side methods applies. They produce different results and are not interchangeable.

Method

How

OData / Fiori handled

Best for

Key User — Custom Fields (F1481)

Fiori UI, no ABAP

Automatically — standard UI, OData, and Fiori field placement wired up by the platform

Simple fields in released views, where standard Fiori UI placement is the goal

Developer — Extension Include

ADT: append to an SAP-provided E_* include structure; extend the view to expose it

Partially — field is in the view; OData exposure still needs a custom Service Binding

Views with a pre-registered extension include (_Extension association visible in ADT); cleanest developer path when available

Developer — Z-table + Extend View

ADT: custom Z-table, basic CDS view on it, extend the standard view with a new association

Manually — you create a Service Definition and Service Binding in ADT

Full developer control; enrichment from external data sources or data with no counterpart in SAP's model

How to choose in practice:

  • Open the Custom Fields app (F1481). If the view appears in the data source list as Released, use the key user path.
  • Open the view in ADT. If you see a pre-defined _Extension association pointing to an E_* include view, SAP has pre-wired an extension point. Add an append to the include structure and extend the view to expose the field, and no Z-table is needed.
  • If neither applies, the view is not in the Custom Fields app (F1481) and has no pre-wired extension include, use the Z-table approach below.

What the worked example uses: the Z-table + Extend View path. This is the most general approach and the one most commonly needed for custom enrichment scenarios. It requires the most manual steps but gives you complete control over the data model.

Worked Example

A manufacturing company needs to add a sustainability certification reference (ZZ_SUSTAIN_CERT_REF) to purchase order items so it is available for Datasphere replication, custom analytical queries and downstream applications built on the extended CDS view.

Step 1, Create the custom extension table. Create a transparent Z-table (ZPOITEM_SUST) with MANDT, EBELN (PurchaseOrder), and EBELP (PurchaseOrderItem) as key fields, plus ZZ_SUSTAIN_CERT_REF as the payload field. Create a basic CDS view (ZI_POItemSustain) on top of it. This table is the data store for the extension; the CDS view makes it joinable from the standard view layer.

Step 2, Extend the interface view:

@AbapCatalog.sqlViewAppendName: 'ZEXPOITEMSUST'
@EndUserText.label: 'Extend PO Item — Sustainability Cert'

extend view I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01
  with ZEX_I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01
  association [0..1] to ZI_POItemSustain as _ZPOItemSustain
    on  $projection.PurchaseOrder     = _ZPOItemSustain.PurchaseOrder
    and $projection.PurchaseOrderItem = _ZPOItemSustain.PurchaseOrderItem
{
  -- Expose the field from the extension table
  _ZPOItemSustain.ZZ_SustainCertRef,

  -- Expose the association so path expressions work downstream
  _ZPOItemSustain
}

Syntax note: I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01 uses the classic define view syntax, so its extension uses extend view Base with ExtensionName { } with a mandatory @AbapCatalog.sqlViewAppendName annotation. Select the Extend View template in ADT. Use $projection.FieldName in association ON conditions to qualify base view fields and avoid ambiguity errors.

Step 3a, Verify at the CDS layer:

With ZEX_I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01 activated, ZZ_SustainCertRef is now part of the extended I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01 view. Verify by opening the view in ADT and pressing F8 (Data Preview). The column should appear alongside standard PO item fields. Add a row to ZPOITEM_SUST for a real PO item first so you have a non-null value to confirm.

Step 3b, Expose via a custom OData service:

The standard SAP purchase order API (API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV) has an explicit contract and does not inherit CDS view extensions. To expose ZZ_SustainCertRef via OData, you need a custom service definition and binding.

Create and Activate the Service Definition

  • Name: ZSD_POITEMSUSTAIN

@EndUserText.label: 'PO Item Sustainability Extension'
define service ZSD_POITEMSUSTAIN {
  expose I_PurchaseOrderItemAPI01 as PurchaseOrderItem;
}

Create, Activate and Publish the Service Binding

  • Name: ZSB_POITEMSUSTAIN
  • Binding Type: OData V4 – Web API
  • Service Definition: ZSD_POITEMSUSTAIN

The editor shows the service URL once published.

Append /$metadata to the service URL and search for ZZ_SustainCertRef. It will appear as a property on the PurchaseOrderItem entity type. Query the entity set for a PO item that has a row in ZPOITEM_SUST to confirm the value is returned.

Joule: The custom OData service published here is the data source for a Joule skill. Register ZSB_POITEMSUSTAIN as a BTP destination, point a Joule skill at that endpoint, and Joule can surface ZZ_SustainCertRef in natural language responses alongside standard PO item data. The CDS extension is the foundation, one field added at the interface layer, surfaced through every consumer that reads from the service.

What this extension does not do automatically: expose the field in SAP's standard A2X API (API_PURCHASEORDER_PROCESS_SRV) or in the standard Fiori UI. For Fiori UI visibility, the same extend view pattern applies to the item-level consumption view that backs your target app.  Identify it in View Browser (F2170) and add an equivalent extension with @UI annotations. For standard API exposure, the supported path is the Custom Fields app (F1481), which handles the service registration as part of the key user extensibility flow.

Performance Considerations

A few principles worth stating upfront, before they become debugging sessions later.

Use associations, not joins, for optional enrichment data. An association resolves only when a consumer navigates it. A join executes unconditionally on every query. For custom enrichment tables — classification data, custom attributes, legacy reference data — associations are almost always the right choice. A poorly placed join on I_JournalEntryItem (backed by ACDOCA with hundreds of millions of rows in production) can have a significant impact on query response time.

Declare cardinality accurately. [0..1] vs [1..1] on an association is not cosmetic. Incorrect cardinality can cause the query optimiser to generate multiply-joining plans, producing duplicate rows or forcing outer joins where inner joins would suffice.

Avoid calculated fields in ON and WHERE clauses. Computed expressions in join conditions prevent HANA from pushing predicates to the storage layer. The result is a scan instead of a seek.

Validate with ST05 and ADT Dependency Analyser after activation. What runs in 200ms on a sandbox with 50,000 rows may behave differently on a production system with 800 million. Test with realistic data volumes before promoting to quality.

Pre-Flight Checklist Before You Extend

Before writing a line of code on any SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition extension:

  • ☐ Base view has C1, C0, or #PUBLIC_LOCAL_API contract, verified in ADT API State tab
  • ☐ View registered in SCFD_REGISTRY, or @Metadata.allowExtensions: true present on the base view
  • ☐ Enhancement category is not #NONE
  • ☐ No GROUP BY or UNION in the base view
  • ☐ Gap type confirmed: standard SAP field (Alt Search in View Browser first) or custom data
  • ☐ Bottom-up propagation plan mapped out, every layer from DB to consumption
  • ☐ Extension object created in ABAP Cloud software component (compiler enforces release contract compliance)
  • ☐ Associations used for optional data, no unconditional joins on high-volume views
  • ☐ Cardinality declared accurately on all associations
  • ☐ Naming convention followed: ZEX_I_*, ZEX_C_*, ZEX_Q_*
  • ☐ Transport dependency order documented, extension activates after base view

Governance Checklist Per Extension

For architect sign-off on any extension going to quality:

  • ☐ Release contract confirmed (ADT + SCFD_REGISTRY)
  • ☐ ABAP Cloud software component used, compiler passes without released-object violations
  • ☐ All VDM layers propagated bottom-up, confirmed end-to-end in the Fiori app and OData service
  • ☐ Performance reviewed, ST05 trace run on production-scale data
  • ☐ Simplification List checked, base objects not deprecated in target release
  • ☐ Downstream consumers inventoried: Fiori apps, SAC, Datasphere, OData clients, Joule skills if applicable
  • ☐ If OData exposure needed: service definition and binding created, BTP destination configured
  • ☐ Transport landscape validated, correct promotion order in dev → QA → prod

Part 2 picks up here: six situations you are likely to encounter on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition projects, with the exact technical detail of what goes wrong and why, and the full architecture chain from CDS extension to working Joule skill, end to end.
