entry.title: Halloween, One Extra Zero and SAP's Tabular AI: Validating Campaign Orders with SAP-RPT-1.6
entry.content:
Halloween is behind us, and many retail chains are already placing their Christmas orders. SAP has announced the availability of SAP-RPT-1.6, tabular orchestration and the SAP-RPT playground API, and tabular AI had hands-on sessions at SAP TechEd 2026. Following SAP's latest announcement (SAP-RPT-1.6, Tabular Orchestration, and RPT Playground API: Now Available), I applied SAP-RPT-1.6 to a problem that comes back every year in retail: campaign orders.

One extra zero

In every major campaign (Halloween, Christmas, Diwali or any other peak buying season), the marketing team of a large retailer places thousands of order lines to refresh the look of hundreds of stores: banners, vinyls, displays, decorations. Each store has its own size, format and sales volume, and every line is filled in under time pressure.

At that volume, errors are inevitable: one extra zero (4 banners become 40), two swapped digits, units entered instead of packs, a hypermarket quantity in a neighbourhood store, or the same material ordered twice. None of them looks serious on the order screen. The trouble starts afterwards.

  • Goods receipts are posted automatically and have to be reversed.
  • Invoices are generated automatically and have to be rejected, and journal entries reconciled again.
  • It is not just marketing: IT has to step in to correct orders and cancel goods receipts.
  • If the error crosses a month-end close, as it does with Halloween, the reversals spill over into the following months.
  • The supplier produces and ships too much material, or a store is left without its campaign branding.

One extra zero multiplies the spend on that line by ten, ties up several teams for days and keeps the campaign's books open for weeks. Across thousands of lines and hundreds of stores, the error is no longer an anecdote: it is money lost, margin gone and teams firefighting at the busiest time of the year.

What I built

Drawing on my experience in the industry, I built a campaign order validator with a Fiori look and feel that checks the campaign order before it reaches SAP S/4HANA. It uses synthetic data, calls SAP-RPT-1.6 live through the SAP-RPT playground and creates the purchase orders in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. The flow has three steps:

Raw file uploaded by manager.

  1. Upload: the campaign manager uploads the file with every order line, one per store and material.
  2. Duplicates: a deterministic rule detects the same material ordered twice for the same store, and the user decides which line stays.
  3. Quantities: SAP-RPT receives, as context, a set of correct orders from previous campaigns together with each store's characteristics (format, floor area, sales, region). From that, it predicts how much each store should order of each material. If the quantity entered falls outside a reasonable range, the line is flagged and the user corrects it, or accepts it with a reason.

Every flagged line comes with its explanation: the expected quantity, the accepted range and the similar stores it was compared with. In the end, only validated lines become purchase orders in S/4HANA, through its standard API.

The results speak for themselves: in my tests with synthetic data, it caught 100 % of the quantity errors injected and every duplicate, with only 1 % false alarms.

Quantity check with the explanation of a flagged line

Purchase Order created from the app

 

Today this is an MVP: production would require work on governance, security, load testing and user experience. But the scenario is real, integrated end to end with S/4HANA, and it addresses a problem that consumer products and retail companies face in every campaign.

Why tabular AI

This scenario shows why tabular AI wins where other approaches fall short.

  • An LLM is not the right tool. General-purpose language models struggle to predict numbers from structured data: they mix up units and give different answers to the same question. I saw this first-hand in an earlier experiment comparing SAP-RPT-1 with several AI assistants.
  • A custom machine learning model is expensive. It has to be trained and, above all, retrained every time marketing trends, campaign materials or the store network change. For a seasonal process, that effort rarely pays off.
  • SAP-RPT learns on the spot. It receives examples of correct orders together with the lines to check, and predicts without any prior training. When the campaign changes, the examples change, not the model.

A problem that used to require a data science project is now solved with an API call.

Validate at the source

That is why the value goes beyond helping the person who fills in the order. Validating before the order reaches SAP avoids the downstream work in goods receipt, finance and IT, and protects the month-end close just when the campaign leaves the least room.

Closing

SAP's tabular AI now makes it possible to tackle everyday ERP problems that were never worth solving before, integrated with S/4HANA from day one. Retail campaigns are only the beginning: any mass upload with an "expected" volume, such as store replenishment, promotions or intercompany orders, follows the same pattern.

How many orders does your organisation correct after each campaign? Share it in the comments. And if you would like to see the demo or explore how to apply this to your processes, reach out: I will be happy to talk.

entry.title: Building an MCP Server with SAP CAP on SAP BTP: AI Assistant for SAP S/4HANA (Part 1 of 2)
entry.content:
Introduction

An earlier post, Connecting SAP S/4HANA to AI with MCP and SAP BTP, described a small MCP server in Python that let an AI assistant read SAP S/4HANA data through OData. The approach worked, but every part of it was custom code: a custom login check, custom logging and a custom deployment.

This two-part series rebuilds the same assistant the SAP way, with the SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) on SAP BTP. The result is one CAP application that answers questions about SAP S/4HANA data, both through an MCP endpoint for AI tools and through standard OData.

  • Part 1 (this post): the architecture, the CAP project file by file, connecting to S/4HANA, the MCP endpoint, login with the user's own token, and deployment.
  • Part 2: securing the application and adding AI-powered SAP Basis monitoring over RFC.

This post is for SAP Basis, BTP and integration people who know S/4HANA and want a working pattern for connecting AI to it. Full-time development experience is not required; the places where SAP Basis knowledge matters are highlighted along the way.

Why SAP CAP instead of a hand-written MCP server

CAP provides, out of the box, the capabilities that previously had to be built by hand, in a form that other SAP teams recognise and can support.

Topic Hand-written Python server SAP CAP application

LoginCustom API key checkXSUAA login and roles, checked by CAP for every request
Who may do whatOne key for everyoneRole collections in the BTP cockpit, e.g. User
Connecting to S/4HANACustom HTTP calls and credentialsCAP remote services through a BTP destination and the Cloud Connector
Audit trailPrint statements@cap-js/audit-logging, SAP's standard plugin (Part 2)
Personal dataNot described@PersonalData annotations in the CDS model
Deploymentcf push per appOne MTA archive: mbt build and cf deploy

The tools themselves stay almost the same. The difference is everything around them: login, roles, connectivity, logging and deployment now follow the SAP standard.

Architecture

Users only ever open the approuter. It handles the login and passes the user's token to the chat website, which calls the CAP app with that same token. The CAP app reaches S/4HANA through the BTP destination and the Cloud Connector. Nothing stores business data on the way.

Prerequisites

  • SAP BTP subaccount with Cloud Foundry enabled, and entitlements for Authorization and Trust Management (XSUAA), Destination and Connectivity.
  • SAP Cloud Connector connected to the subaccount, exposing the S/4HANA Gateway (/sap/opu/odata/).
  • A BTP destination of type HTTP to S/4HANA through the Cloud Connector (ProxyType: OnPremise).
  • SAP S/4HANA with the standard OData APIs activated in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, e.g. API_BUSINESS_PARTNER and API_SALES_ORDER_SRV.
  • A technical SAP user for the destination. Read-only authorizations only; more on this in Part 2.
  • On your laptop: Node.js 22, @SAP/cds-dk (npm i -g @SAP/cds-dk), the Cloud MTA Build Tool (npm i -g mbt) and the Cloud Foundry CLI with the MultiApps plugin.

The project, file by file

The project is created with cds init and keeps CAP's standard layout. The following files make it a CAP project and are the best starting point:

sap-ai-assistant-cap/
├─ package.json          CAP dependencies and the cds configuration (remote services, auth, audit log)
├─ srv/
│  ├─ s4-service.cds     the service: entities and one function per tool, @requires: 'User'
│  ├─ s4-service.js      the handlers behind those functions
│  ├─ external/          imported SAP API definitions (cds import)
│  ├─ server.js          start-up: destination, MCP endpoint
│  ├─ mcp.js             the MCP endpoint /mcp
│  └─ sap/               the tools, the allow-list of SAP APIs, metadata reading
├─ app/
│  ├─ router/            the approuter: the only address users open (login)
│  └─ web/               the chat website
├─ xs-security.json      scopes and role collections
└─ mta.yaml              how everything is built and deployed together

The three that matter most:

  • srv/s4-service.cds declares the service: who may use it, and which functions it offers.
  • package.json, in its cds section, declares where SAP is, how login works and where audit entries go. It's configuration, not code.
  • mta.yaml puts the CAP app, the website and the approuter into one deployable archive, together with the BTP services they need.

A quick way to tell a CAP project from "Node.js code that calls SAP" is cds watch. It starts the whole service locally, with mocked login, from these files alone.

Connecting CAP to SAP S/4HANA

CAP reaches S/4HANA through a remote service that points at the BTP destination. No URL, user or password is in the code; the destination and the Cloud Connector handle all of that.

First, import the API definition of the Business Partner API (the EDMX from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub):

cds import API_BUSINESS_PARTNER.edmx --as cds

Then declare the remote services in package.json. The destination name is set at deployment, not in the code:

"cds": {
  "requires": {
    "API_BUSINESS_PARTNER": { "kind": "odata-v2", "model": "srv/external/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER" },
    "S4HANA": { "kind": "odata-v2", "credentials": { "path": "/sap/opu/odata" } }
  }
}

In srv/server.js, every remote service gets the destination from an environment variable that mta.yaml fills in:

const destination = process.env.SAP_DESTINATION
for (const conf of Object.values(cds.env.requires)) {
  if (conf?.kind === 'odata-v2') conf.credentials = { ...conf.credentials, destination }
}

The application uses two styles of access:

  • Typed CDS queries on imported APIs, e.g. a projection on A_BusinessPartner. CAP translates OData V4 options such as $filter and $select into the V2 call automatically.
  • Raw OData V2 calls for everything else: await s4.send({ method: 'GET', path: 'sap/API_SALES_ORDER_SRV/A_SalesOrder?$top=5' }). This lets the tools work with any allowed API without importing each one.

Two Basis details to check before investigating the code:

  1. Cloud Connector resource: the path /sap/opu/odata/ must be exposed, with "path and all sub-paths".
  2. The services must be active in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE. A service that isn't answers with a 403 or 404 that looks like an authorization problem.

Tools as CAP functions, and the MCP endpoint

Every tool exists once and is offered through two doors: as a CAP function over OData, and as an MCP tool at /mcp. Both give exactly the same answer text, because both call the same JavaScript function.

The service in srv/s4-service.cds:

@requires: 'User'
@path    : '/odata/v4/s4'
service S4Service {

  @readonly
  entity BusinessPartners as projection on bp.A_BusinessPartner {
    key BusinessPartner, BusinessPartnerFullName as Name, CreationDate
  };

  function list_sap_services(search : String)                           returns LargeString;
  function query_sap(![service] : String, entity_set : String,
                     ![filter] : String, ![select] : String, top : Integer) returns LargeString;
  function find_sap_data(question : String, top : Integer)               returns LargeString;
  function search_business_partners(name : String, top : Integer)       returns LargeString;
  function get_sales_order(sales_order : String)                         returns LargeString;
  // ... one function per tool
}

@requires: 'User' is the whole authorization check for the OData door. CAP refuses any request without a valid login (401) or without the User role (403) before any application code runs. @readonlyand the absence of any create/update function make the service read-only by design.

The MCP endpoint is a small Express route in srv/mcp.js, using the official SDK @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. It sits behind CAP's own login middleware, so the same check applies:

app.post('/mcp', ...cds.middlewares.before, requireUser,
         express.json({ limit: '1mb' }), handle)

handle creates a stateless MCP server for each request. It lists the tools (each marked readOnlyHint: true) and runs a tool by calling the same function the OData door uses. Being stateless means several app instances can serve the same chat without shared sessions.

For /mcp, cds.middlewares.before is the key line: it gives a custom route the same login, user context and audit hooks as CAP's own services.

Answering plain-English questions from SAP's own metadata

Fixed tools only answer the questions that were anticipated at design time. To go further, the assistant gets four general tools:

Tool What it does

list_sap_servicesLists the SAP APIs the assistant may use: an allow-list, cross-checked against the services that are really registered in the system (/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE)
describe_sap_serviceReads an API's $metadata: its entity sets, fields with their SAP labels, and links
query_sapReads rows with $filter, $select, $orderby and $top, with a hard limit on rows and answer size
find_sap_dataTakes one plain-English question and works out the service, entity set and filters itself

find_sap_data is the most powerful of the four. It reads every allowed service's $metadata (cached for an hour) and scores each entity set against the words in the question. It uses SAP's own descriptions and field labels, so "how many sales orders were created last month" finds A_SalesOrder and CreationDate without a single hardcoded mapping. The answer always states exactly what it queried, so a user can check it.

The project follows a strict rule: no company data, sample IDs or hardcoded values in the code. Every number, name and ID in an answer comes from SAP at the moment of the question. Adding a new standard API is a configuration change (SAP_EXTRA_SERVICES), not a code change.

Login and roles: the user's own token, no shared key

The biggest change from the Python version: there is no shared API key any more. Every request carries the signed-in user's own login token.

  1. The user opens the approuter address, the only address users ever open. The approuter sends them to the login page of the subaccount's identity provider.
  2. After login, the approuter passes the user's XSUAA token on to the chat website (forwardAuthToken: true).
  3. The website calls the CAP app's /mcp with that same token.
  4. CAP checks the token and the User role on every request, for OData and MCP alike.

The roles are defined in xs-security.json:

{
  "scopes": [{ "name": "$XSAPPNAME.User", "description": "Use the SAP assistant" }],
  "role-templates": [{ "name": "User", "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.User"] }],
  "role-collections": [{
    "name": "SAP AI Assistant CAP User",
    "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.User"]
  }]
}

An administrator assigns the role collection to users in the BTP cockpit (Security → Users). Because the token belongs to a person, CAP knows who asked what, which the audit log in Part 2 builds on.

In mta.yaml, the login service's redirect-uris are also restricted to the approuter's own address. As a result, no other app on the shared cfapps domain can receive a login result meant for this one.

Important: once a role collection is assigned to users, you can't add roles to it through xs-security.json. The XSUAA service update fails with "Adding role-template-references to role collection ... is restricted". Create a new role collection with a new name instead.

Build and deploy

Everything goes to Cloud Foundry as one MTA archive. mta.yaml describes three apps and the services they use:

Module What it is Binds

...-srvThe CAP app: OData and /mcpXSUAA, Destination, Connectivity
...-webThe chat websiteXSUAA
...-routerThe approuter, the only address users openXSUAA

System-specific values are kept out of git in a small extension file, config.mtaext:

_schema-version: '3.1'
ID: sap-ai-assistant-cap.config
extends: sap-ai-assistant-cap
parameters:
  sap-destination: <your BTP destination name>
  router-host: <the host name users open>

Then build and deploy:

npm ci
mbt build
cf deploy mta_archives/sap-ai-assistant-cap_1.0.0.mtar -e config.mtaext

Finally, assign the role collection to the users in the BTP cockpit.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them:

  1. Build timeout. On a laptop, the website's build took longer than mbt's default 10 minutes, so an old archive was deployed without any warning. Fix: build-parameters: timeout: 40m on that module.
  2. Stack deprecation. Cloud Foundry warned that cflinuxfs4 is deprecated. Fix: stack: cflinuxfs5 on each module, then rebuild and redeploy (a restage alone doesn't change it).
  3. Role collections are frozen once assigned. See the login section: create a new collection rather than changing an assigned one.
  4. Duplicate downloads. When a new version of the project zip is downloaded, the browser may save it as ... (1).zip, and the old archive is easily unpacked by mistake. A quick Select-String for a new line of code before mbt build saves a lot of confusion.

The result

Users open one address, log in with their normal company account, and ask questions about SAP S/4HANA data in plain English. Every answer is read live from SAP at the moment of the question.

Key points for SAP Basis consultants:

  • One login, checked twice. The website checks the token, and the CAP app checks it again for every request. Someone who finds the CAP app's own address still can't get in without a valid token and the role.
  • Nothing stored. There's no database; every answer comes from SAP when it's asked, so there's no copy of business data in BTP.
  • Read-only by design. The service has no write functions and its entities are @readonly.

Conclusion and what's next

Rebuilding the MCP server with SAP CAP took more thought than writing a Python script, but the result is something an SAP team can own:

  • standard login and roles;
  • connectivity through the destination and the Cloud Connector;
  • one deployable archive.

The AI side, the MCP endpoint, turned out to be the smallest part. Doing it properly on BTP was the real work.

Part 2 covers what it takes to make the application safe to put in front of real users:

  • a line-by-line security review of the code, including a text pattern that could freeze the app;
  • data rules for the SAP APIs, request limits and the SAP audit log;
  • AI-powered SAP Basis monitoring over RFC, with a dashboard for SM51, SM04, SM58 and SM37.

Thanks for reading. If you've built something similar with CAP and MCP, or have questions about any of the steps, feel free to share your experience in the comments.

entry.title: Your MCP server is open for contributions, but do your users and their agents know about it?
entry.content:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are essential building blocks in agentic engineering scenarios. The MCP protocol is used in the architecture of AI-native or AI-enabled software solutions, and also by the developers building and maintaining said solutions.

What happens though, when the MCP server is not working as expected? What if a feature is missing? Can the MCP client, usually an agent harness, guide its user into finding support and/or feedback channels, or even the contribution guidelines of the project behind the server, when it is open source / InnerSource? Can it contribute bug fixes or missing features? The answer is: No, unless the server is prepared for that.

In this blog post you will find the results of an experiment with a demo MCP server created to show a proof-of-concept for enabling such MCP server "introspection" scenarios, learn how the server works, and get access to the source code to try it yourself!

Why is this important? Open Source and InnerSource User Experience

Here is a topic that I think we in the open source and InnerSource communities don't discuss enough.

I recall my first contribution to an InnerSource project at SAP. It was an internal multi-purpose dashboard called Bridge. This was back when GitHub was still a novelty at SAP and ABAP was king (long live ABAP, seriously!).

Even with the nice experience I had, with the apps available on this dashboard, some features were still missing. What to do from here? Report a missing feature and wait? Can I even find how to do that, without digging too much?

Well, this particular internal tool had something I had only seen so far in (some) open source projects: a clear invitation to contribute, directly found in the tool's user interface.

Reverse mockup of the user interface (UI) of Bridge, created with Copilot Chat - an invitation to contribute is easily found directly on the UI

The journey from user to contributor could be taken directly from the tool, in other words, InnerSource was part of the user experience, not just something hidden behind the scenes, or revealed only to those persistent enough to dig up the source code repository.

The idea of representing open source and InnerSource use cases as part of the user experience of a software solution, or user-facing content, is not entirely new. Nevertheless, the concept does not even have a name yet (to my best knowledge), so I'll coin here the twin terms: Open Source User Experience and InnerSource User Experience.

Such use cases, some of which are not exclusive to open source and / or InnerSource, include:

  • discovering where to ask questions or discuss the software with the project team, other users or interested parties,
  • discovering how to provide feedback, report issues or request new features,
  • and, of course, discovering how to access the source code and perhaps eventually contribute back to it.

This topic is not without "prior art", you can refer to Contributor Personas & Pathways and Contributor Journey Optimization, but it is definitely not explored as much as it should be.

In the example I described above, we saw InnerSource User Experience in action for a "traditional" web application user interface, but how could this be applied to an "AI Native" user interface, such as a user interacting with a remote service through an agent harness (e.g., the Joule Work desktop app, or Claude Code)?

This is what we will explore next.

The "testbed" MCP server

Our open source / InnerSource user experience experiment will need a real-world-like MCP server to serve as a testbed.

I've chosen a use case that is close to my home turf and implemented, with the help of some invisible robots, an MCP server that enables clients to access a catalog of InnerSource projects. This use case is inspired by the InnerSource Pattern "InnerSource (Projects) Portal".

To cater to the use case of listing InnerSource projects, our MCP server will offer a single tool, "list-innersource-projects". It brings a list of fictitious projects containing, for each entry: project name, description, links to source code repository,  support channels and contribution guidelines, and finally, the number of forks.

Let's see how this looks like in action, testing it on the Joule Work desktop app:

Screenshot of Joule Work desktop app listing InnerSource projects

It does not contain the number of stars. This is, on purpose, a missing feature.

The challenge: Taking users where they need to go, when things go wrong

So let's see what happens when I tell my agent to "sort the projects by number of stars":

"Tinkering, blooping, buying RAM..., done: The InnerSource projects data doesn't include a star count — the only popularity metric available is forks. The API also only supports sorting by name or forks.

Would you like me to sort the list by forks instead?"

Note that while I'm showing results in this post using the Joule Work desktop app as an agent harness and MCP client, I also tested it with Claude Code, and I expect to have similar results with other combinations of harnesses and models.

Now, from here, many users would simply say "what a bummer" and move on with their lives without their desired sorting. Users with a continuous improvement mindset may start asking the agent stuff like: "report sorting by stars as a feature" or "where can I give feedback?"; while curious tech-savvy users would likely prompt next: "take me to the source code" or even "contribute this feature to the server".

That would not take the user anywhere, unless the maintainers of the server thought about this ahead of time. So let's see if we can enable our server to take these users where they want to go.

The first (kind of) failed attempt at solving the problem

After learning a bit about the Model Context Protocol, my first instinct was to add some general instructions to the server metadata about how the agent should behave and also present the contribution guidelines as a server resource.

I could not find where to provide those general instructions (that's on me, it is possible), so I have tried adding that to the description of the tool "list-innersource-projects".

That was my first implementation. It kind of failed.

What I wanted to achieve was, when prompting to sort by stars, a response along the lines of: "I can't do that, but the server accepts contributions, should I contribute that feature for you?".

Instead, I got the same response as before, BUT, if I came with the explicit intent to contribute, like prompting "Can we contribute this as a feature?", the agent guided me there, and even implemented the feature and sent a pull request on my behalf.

Getting there, with the help of some robot friends

From there, I did what we are expected to do when vibe-coding these days, don't tell your coding agent what to do, tell it what you want to achieve.

A nice learning experience for me, and it came with a somewhat hacky solution. Here is what it implemented in 4 layers (its own words):

  1. Server instructions (the standing policy) - the server passes instructions to the client in the response to the server/discover query. These instructions tell the client about the open source / InnerSource features of this server, and how to react to missing features.
  2. Declared capabilities on tool responses - the response of the tool "list-innersource-projects" is a JSON data structure containing, in addition to the list of projects, a "capabilities" property. Although it looks like something a deterministic JSON parser would take and act on, it is actually telling the Large Language Model (LLM), through the client, that accepting contributions is one of the capabilities of this server.
  3. An executable action - the server offers an additional tool, "propose-contribution". Calling it does not change the state of the server in any way, but returns information to the client on how to perform a contribution.
  4. Loud, actionable failures - if the server receives a request for projects sorted by an unsupported property, it responds with an "unsupported_capability" payload carrying the requested capability, the supported contract, the contribution path, and an explicit "nextStep".

Oh yeah! That's the Open Source and InnerSource User Experience in action. The client informs the user that the requested action is not possible, but also that the project (our server) accepts contribution, and offers help in proposing the missing feature.

Saying "Yes" here starts the journey of submitting an AI-assisted contribution to fill the gap in the server.

Conclusion and Outlook

Our little experiment showed that the state-of-the-art of agent harnesses, as MCP clients, do not drive contributions of missing features on their own. Even if you come with an intent to contribute, the harness still needs a way to discover the path to follow to make that happen. On the other hand, it also showed that it is possible to drive contributions from the server side using the current state of open standards, which is exactly what is within the sphere of control of the server's maintainers.

With this blog post, I didn't just want to demonstrate it is possible to guide users into becoming contributors, but also motivate people to think about incorporating open source and InnerSource in the user experience of what they are building. In particular, I'd like to bring this to agentic experiences.

There are still challenges ahead, like testing whether this would work if you had several MCP servers open for contributions available to the same client. Would it be able to detect in which server a feature is missing? Would it propose the contribution to the correct server and follow its corresponding contribution guidelines? Those are questions we will need to answer, in order to put this concept in use in the real world.

We also should watch carefully how the open standards for agentic engineering evolve, such as through the introduction of MCP Server Cards, which could provide open source and/or InnerSource related information to the client. Here is where the open source and InnerSource communities should also engage and influence the development of such open standards to accommodate their use cases.
